\label{thm:main}
For every $\alpha$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:closed}
  \Upsilon_A(t)=\frac{e^{t}\bigl(\cosh2\alpha t-\cosh t\bigr)}{\sinh 2t}
  =\tfrac12\bigl(\operatorname{csch}t+\operatorname{sech}t\bigr)
   \bigl(\cosh2\alpha t-\cosh t\bigr),\qquad A=\alpha^2 .
\end{equation}
Equivalently, coefficientwise,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:coef}
  L_n^{\mathrm{diag}}=\frac{4^n}{n(n+1)}
  \Bigl[\mathcal B_{n+1}\bigl(\tfrac{3+2\alpha}4\bigr)
       +\mathcal B_{n+1}\bigl(\tfrac{3-2\alpha}4\bigr)
       -\mathcal B_{n+1}(1)-\mathcal B_{n+1}\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)\Bigr].
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:contiguity}
On the diagonal, as an identity of formal Laurent series at $Z=\infty$,
\[
F(Z+4)\,Z(Z+2)=F(Z)\bigl((Z+1)^2-4A\bigr).
\]
Equivalently, $\mathcal G(Z):=\Gamma(Z)F(Z)$ satisfies, in the same
formal sense,
\[
\mathcal G(Z+4)=(Z+1)(Z+3)\bigl((Z+1)^2-4A\bigr)\mathcal G(Z).
\]
For half-odd-integer $\alpha$ the first identity is an identity of
rational functions of $Z$ and the second one of meromorphic functions,
by Theorem~\ref{thm:halfinteger}.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:specials}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $\Upsilon_A=\upsilon_1\cosh2\alpha t+\upsilon_0$ with
  $\upsilon_0(t)$, $\upsilon_1(t)$ independent of $\alpha$;
  coefficientwise, for $k\ge1$,
  $[A^k]\Upsilon_A=\frac{2^{2k-1}}{(2k)!}t^{2k-2}[A^1]\Upsilon_A$.
\item[(ii)] $\Upsilon_{1/4}\equiv0$: there is no correction in the
  Chebyshev cases $\alpha=\beta=\pm\frac12$.
\item[(iii)] In the Legendre case,
  $\Upsilon_0(t)=\frac12\bigl(\operatorname{sech}t-\tanh\frac t2-1\bigr)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:R}
With $g_n$ and $\Phi$ as in~\eqref{eq:gdef},
\[
  \operatorname{Re}\Phi(t)=\frac{t^2e^t}{\sinh2t},
\]
that is, $\operatorname{Re}g_{2k+1}=(1-2^{2k-1})\mathcal B_{2k}$ and
$\operatorname{Re}g_{2k}=\frac12(2k-1)\mathsf E_{2k-2}$.  In particular
$\nu_2(\operatorname{Re}g_n)=-1$ for every $n\ge1$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:dyadic}
For every $k\ge1$, $\operatorname{Im}g_{2k}=0$, so that $W$ is an even
power series.  For every $m\ge0$,
\[
  \nu_2(w_m)=-2\,\nu_2\bigl((2m)!\bigr),\qquad\text{that is,}\qquad
  \bigl((2m)!\bigr)^2w_m\in\mathbb Z_2^\times .
\]
Equivalently, for every $r\ge1$,
\[
 \nu_2\bigl(\operatorname{Im}g_{2r-1}\bigr)=-H_r,
 \qquad
 \nu_2\bigl([A^1B^0]\kappa_r\bigr)=-E_r ,
\]
with $\kappa_r$ defined by~\eqref{eq:kappadef}.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:imclosed}
As formal series in $Z^{-1}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:formal-tangent}
 \sum_{n\ge1}g_n\,Z^{-n}
 =\frac1{16}\,\psi'\!\Bigl(\frac{Z+1}4\Bigr)
 -\frac1{16}\,\psi'\!\Bigl(\frac{Z+3}4\Bigr)
 +\frac14\,\psi'\!\Bigl(\frac{Z+1}2\Bigr)
 -\frac i2\,\widehat Q_\Gamma(Z),
\end{equation}
where each trigamma function $\psi'$ stands for its asymptotic
(Bernoulli) expansion, and $\widehat Q_\Gamma$ is the unique formal
series without constant term that solves the central-difference
equation
\[
  \widehat Q_\Gamma(s+1)-\widehat Q_\Gamma(s-1)
  =-\frac{(2s-1)}{4s(s-1)}
   \left[\frac{\Gamma(s/2)}{\Gamma((1+s)/2)}\right]^2,
  \qquad s=\frac{1-Z}2,
\]
the right-hand side being replaced by its asymptotic expansion in
powers of $s^{-1}$.  In particular
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Imgclosed}
 \operatorname{Im}g_n=-\tfrac12\,\widehat q_n\qquad(n\ge1),
\end{equation}
where $\widehat q_n$ is the coefficient of $Z^{-n}$ in
$\widehat Q_\Gamma$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:hankelhalf}
For $\alpha=\ell+\frac12$,
\[
  a_k\bigl(\ell+\tfrac12\bigr)=\frac{(\ell+k)!}{(\ell-k)!\,k!\,2^k}
  \quad(0\le k\le\ell),\qquad a_k\bigl(\ell+\tfrac12\bigr)=0\quad(k>\ell),
\]
so that $\sum_ka_k(\ell+\frac12)\xi^k=y_\ell(\xi)$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Since $4\alpha^2=(2\ell+1)^2$, the product in the definition of $a_k$ is
\[
\prod_{j<k}\bigl((2\ell+1)^2-(2j+1)^2\bigr)
=\prod_{j<k}(2\ell-2j)(2\ell+2j+2)=4^k\frac{\ell!}{(\ell-k)!}
\frac{(\ell+k)!}{\ell!}
\]
for $k\le\ell$, and it vanishes for $k>\ell$.  Dividing by $8^kk!$ gives
the stated value.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:bessel}
For $n\ge0$, with the convention $y_{-1}(x)=1$,
\[
  \text{(a)}\quad x^2y_n'(x)=(nx-1)y_n(x)+y_{n-1}(x),
  \qquad
  \text{(b)}\quad y_{n+1}(x)=(2n+1)x\,y_n(x)+y_{n-1}(x).
\]
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Both identities follow by comparing coefficients in the defining sum;
they are classical~\cite{KrallFrink,Burchnall,DunsterEtAl}.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- definitionx-1: body_md -->
$\displaystyle
 C_\ell(\xi)=\tfrac12\Bigl(q\,y_{\ell-1}(p\xi)y_\ell(q\xi)
                        +p\,y_\ell(p\xi)y_{\ell-1}(q\xi)\Bigr)$,
which is real because the two terms are complex conjugate.
<!-- end definitionx-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:step3}
$\xi^2\Pi_\ell'(\xi)+\bigl(1-2\ell \xi\bigr)\Pi_\ell(\xi)=C_\ell(\xi)$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Put $U=y_\ell(p\xi)$, $V=y_\ell(q\xi)$, $U_-=y_{\ell-1}(p\xi)$, $V_-=y_{\ell-1}(q\xi)$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:bessel}(a) at $x=p\xi$ reads $p\,\xi^2U'=(\ell p\xi-1)U+U_-$, and similarly for $V$.  Hence
\begin{multline*}
  \xi^2\Pi_\ell'=\xi^2(U'V+UV')
  =\frac{(\ell p\xi-1)U+U_-}{p}\,V+U\,\frac{(\ell q\xi-1)V+V_-}{q}\\
  =\Bigl(2\ell \xi-\frac1p-\frac1q\Bigr)UV+\frac{U_-V}p+\frac{UV_-}q .
\end{multline*}
By \eqref{eq:pq}, $\frac1p+\frac1q=1$, $\frac1p=\frac q2$ and $\frac1q=\frac p2$, so the right-hand side is $(2\ell \xi-1)\Pi_\ell+C_\ell$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:step4}
$C_{\ell+2}=C_\ell+(4\ell+2)\,\xi\,\Pi_\ell$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
With $U_+=y_{\ell+1}(p\xi)$, $U_{++}=y_{\ell+2}(p\xi)$ and similarly for $V$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:bessel}(b) gives $U_{++}=(2\ell+3)p\xi U_++U$ and
$V_{++}=(2\ell+3)q\xi V_++V$.  Therefore
\[
  2C_{\ell+2}=qU_+V_{++}+pU_{++}V_+
  =(2\ell+3)\xi\,(p^2+q^2)\,U_+V_+\;+\;qU_+V+pUV_+ ,
\]
and the first term vanishes by \eqref{eq:pq}.  Applying
Lemma~\ref{lem:bessel}(b) once more, $U_+=(2\ell+1)p\xi U+U_-$ and
$V_+=(2\ell+1)q\xi V+V_-$, so
\[
  qU_+V+pUV_+=2(2\ell+1)pq\,\xi\,UV+\bigl(qU_-V+pUV_-\bigr)
             =4(2\ell+1)\xi\,\Pi_\ell+2C_\ell ,
\]
using $pq=2$.  Dividing by $2$ gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:gstep}
$\xi^2\Pi_{\ell+2}'+\bigl[1-(2\ell+4)\xi\bigr]\Pi_{\ell+2}
 =\xi^2\Pi_\ell'+\bigl[1+(2\ell+2)\xi\bigr]\Pi_\ell$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:step3} the left side is $C_{\ell+2}$ and the right
side is $C_\ell+(4\ell+2)\xi \Pi_\ell$; apply Proposition~\ref{prop:step4}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:basis}
$Z\,e_n=e_{n-1}+n\,e_n$ for $n\ge1$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
$Ze_n=\bigl((Z-n)+n\bigr)e_n$ and $(Z-n)e_n=e_{n-1}$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:Frec}
$F_{\ell+2}(Z)\,(Z-2\ell-4)=F_\ell(Z)\,(Z+2\ell+2)$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Write $F_\ell=\sum_nG_n^{(\ell)}e_n$ with $G^{(\ell)}_0=1$.  By
Lemma~\ref{lem:basis}, for any constant $c$,
\[
  (Z-c)F_\ell=Z-c+G_1^{(\ell)}
  +\sum_{m\ge1}\Bigl(G^{(\ell)}_{m+1}+(m-c)G^{(\ell)}_m\Bigr)e_m .
\]
Since $G^{(\ell)}_0=1$ for every $\ell$, the terms in $Z$ agree on the two
sides of the claimed identity, and comparing coefficients of $e_m$ (and the
constant, which is the case $m=0$) shows that the identity is equivalent to
\[
  G^{(\ell+2)}_{m+1}+(m-2\ell-4)G^{(\ell+2)}_m
  =G^{(\ell)}_{m+1}+(m+2\ell+2)G^{(\ell)}_m
  \qquad(m\ge0).
\]
Multiplying by $\xi^m$ and summing, and using
$\sum_mG_{m+1}\xi^m=(\Pi-1)/\xi$ and $\sum_mmG_m\xi^m=\xi\Pi'$, this is exactly
Corollary~\ref{cor:gstep} after multiplication by $\xi$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:base}
$F_0=1$ and $F_1(Z)=\dfrac{Z}{Z-2}$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
$y_0(x)=1$ gives $\Pi_0=1$, so $G_0=1$ and $G_n=0$ for $n\ge1$.  $y_1(x)=1+x$
gives $\Pi_1(\xi)=(1+p\xi)(1+q\xi)=1+2\xi+2\xi^2$, so
\[
F_1=1+\frac2{Z-1}+\frac2{(Z-1)(Z-2)}   =\frac{Z^2-Z}{(Z-1)(Z-2)}=\frac Z{Z-2}.
\]
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:halfinteger}
For every $\ell\ge0$, with $\zeta=Z/4$,
\[
  F_\ell(Z)=\mathcal M_\ell(Z):=
  \frac{\Gamma\bigl(\zeta-\frac\ell2\bigr)\,
        \Gamma\bigl(\zeta+\frac{\ell+1}2\bigr)}
       {\Gamma(\zeta)\,\Gamma\bigl(\zeta+\frac12\bigr)} .
\]
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
By the functional equation of $\Gamma$,
\[
  \frac{\mathcal M_{\ell+2}}{\mathcal M_\ell}
  =\frac{\Gamma(\zeta-\frac\ell2-1)}{\Gamma(\zeta-\frac\ell2)}
   \cdot\frac{\Gamma(\zeta+\frac{\ell+3}2)}{\Gamma(\zeta+\frac{\ell+1}2)}
  =\frac{\zeta+\frac{\ell+1}2}{\zeta-\frac{\ell+2}2}
  =\frac{Z+2\ell+2}{Z-2\ell-4},
\]
which is Proposition~\ref{prop:Frec}.  For the base cases, $\mathcal M_0=1$ and
\[
\mathcal M_1=\frac{\Gamma(\zeta-\frac12)}{\Gamma(\zeta+\frac12)}
\frac{\Gamma(\zeta+1)}{\Gamma(\zeta)}=\frac{\zeta}{\zeta-\frac12}
=\frac Z{Z-2}, 
\]
matching Lemma~\ref{lem:base}.  Induction in steps of two along each parity class completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:degree}
For arbitrary weights $p,q$, each coefficient $L_n$ of $\log F$ is a
polynomial in $(A,B)$ of total degree at most $n$.  In particular
$\deg_AL_n^{\mathrm{diag}}\le n$.  Moreover the right-hand side of
\eqref{eq:coef} is a polynomial in $A$ of degree at most
$\lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor\le n$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
$a_k(\nu)$ is a polynomial in $\nu^2$ of degree $k$, so
$a_l(\alpha)a_{n-l}(\beta)$, and hence $G_n$, is a polynomial in $(A,B)$
of total degree at most $n$.  Since
\[
e_n=\sum_{m\ge n}\genfrac{\{}{\}}{0pt}{}{m}{n}Z^{-m}
\]
with $\genfrac{\{}{\}}{0pt}{}{m}{n}$ the Stirling numbers of the
second kind, the coefficients
\[
c_m=\sum_{n\le m}G_n\genfrac{\{}{\}}{0pt}{}{m}{n}
\]
of $F=1+\sum_mc_mZ^{-m}$ have total degree at most $m$, and each $L_n$ is an
isobaric polynomial of weight $n$ in the $c_m$, whence the first two
assertions.  On the other
side $\mathcal B_{n+1}\bigl(\frac{3+2\alpha}4\bigr)+\mathcal B_{n+1}\bigl(\frac{3-2\alpha}4\bigr)$
is even in $\alpha$ of degree at most $n+1$, hence a polynomial in
$A=\alpha^2$ of degree at most $\lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:stirlingexp}
Put
\[
  \mathcal M(\zeta;\alpha)
  =\frac{\Gamma\bigl(\zeta+\frac{1-2\alpha}4\bigr)
         \Gamma\bigl(\zeta+\frac{1+2\alpha}4\bigr)}
        {\Gamma(\zeta)\,\Gamma\bigl(\zeta+\frac12\bigr)} .
\]
Then, for all $\alpha$ and $\zeta\to\infty$,
\[
  \log\mathcal M(\zeta;\alpha)
  \sim\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{\chi_n(\alpha)}{n(n+1)}\,\zeta^{-n},
\]
\[
  \chi_n(\alpha)=\mathcal B_{n+1}\bigl(\tfrac{3+2\alpha}4\bigr)
       +\mathcal B_{n+1}\bigl(\tfrac{3-2\alpha}4\bigr)
       -\mathcal B_{n+1}(1)-\mathcal B_{n+1}\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr).
\]
Moreover $\mathcal M_\ell$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:halfinteger} is the value of
the left-hand quotient at $\alpha=\ell+\frac12$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The classical gamma-quotient expansion, obtained by subtracting
\cite[Eq.~5.11.8]{DLMF} at $h=a$ and $h=b$ (see also
\cite[Sec.~24.2]{DLMF} for the Bernoulli polynomials),

\[
  \log\frac{\Gamma(\zeta+a)}{\Gamma(\zeta+b)}-(a-b)\log\zeta
  \sim\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n(n+1)}
      \bigl(\mathcal B_{n+1}(a)-\mathcal B_{n+1}(b)\bigr)\zeta^{-n}
\]
applies with $a=\frac{1\mp2\alpha}4$ and $b\in\{0,\frac12\}$; the logarithmic
terms cancel because $\frac{1-2\alpha}4+\frac{1+2\alpha}4=\frac12=0+\frac12$.
Using $(-1)^{n+1}\mathcal B_{n+1}(a)=\mathcal B_{n+1}(1-a)$ and
$1-\frac{1\mp2\alpha}4=\frac{3\pm2\alpha}4$, $1-0=1$, $1-\frac12=\frac12$
gives the stated form.  For the second assertion, at
$\alpha=\ell+\frac12$ one has $\frac{1-2\alpha}4=-\frac\ell2$ and
$\frac{1+2\alpha}4=\frac{\ell+1}2$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Fix $n$.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:degree} both sides of \eqref{eq:coef} are
polynomials in $A$ of degree at most $n$.  By Theorem~\ref{thm:halfinteger},
$F=\mathcal M_\ell$ at $\alpha=\ell+\frac12$ for every $\ell\ge0$; both sides
being rational functions of $Z$ there, their expansions at $Z=\infty$
coincide, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:stirlingexp} the coefficients of
$\log\mathcal M_\ell$ are the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:coef} evaluated at
$A=(\ell+\frac12)^2$.  Hence the two polynomials agree at the infinitely many
distinct points $A=(\ell+\frac12)^2$, $\ell=0,1,2,\dots$, and therefore
coincide.  This proves \eqref{eq:coef}.

For \eqref{eq:closed}, sum \eqref{eq:coef} with the generating function
$\sum_k\mathcal B_k(x)u^k/k!=ue^{xu}/(e^u-1)$ at $u=4t$.  The constant and linear
corrections cancel because
$\frac{3+2\alpha}4+\frac{3-2\alpha}4-1-\frac12=0$, and one obtains
\[
  \Upsilon_A(t)=\frac{e^{(3+2\alpha)t}+e^{(3-2\alpha)t}-e^{4t}-e^{2t}}{e^{4t}-1}
  =\frac{2e^{3t}\bigl(\cosh2\alpha t-\cosh t\bigr)}{2e^{2t}\sinh2t},
\]
which is \eqref{eq:closed}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:main} and Lemma~\ref{lem:stirlingexp}, the formal
Laurent series $\log F$ on the diagonal is the Stirling series of
$\Gamma(\zeta+\frac{1-2\alpha}4)\Gamma(\zeta+\frac{1+2\alpha}4)/
\bigl(\Gamma(\zeta)\Gamma(\zeta+\frac12)\bigr)$ with $\zeta=Z/4$, whose ratio
at $\zeta\mapsto\zeta+1$ is
$\bigl(\zeta+\frac{1-2\alpha}4\bigr)\bigl(\zeta+\frac{1+2\alpha}4\bigr)/
\bigl(\zeta(\zeta+\frac12)\bigr)=\bigl((Z+1)^2-4A\bigr)/\bigl(Z(Z+2)\bigr)$.
Thus the ratio identity is first obtained coefficientwise in $Z^{-1}$.
Exponentiating is legitimate because both formal logarithms have zero
constant term, and gives the first displayed contiguity identity.  Multiplying
by the exact quotient
$\Gamma(Z+4)/\Gamma(Z)=Z(Z+1)(Z+2)(Z+3)$ gives the second identity.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:borel}
Conversely, the contiguity of Corollary~\ref{cor:contiguity} determines
\eqref{eq:closed}.  For $f=\sum_{n\ge1}c_nZ^{-n}$ put
$\mathfrak Bf(t)=\sum_nc_nt^{n-1}/(n-1)!$; then
$\mathfrak B[f(Z+c)]=e^{-ct}\mathfrak Bf$ and
$\mathfrak B\bigl[\log\frac{Z+a}{Z+b}\bigr]=(e^{-bt}-e^{-at})/t$, both term by
term.  Applying $\mathfrak B$ to
$\log F(Z+4)-\log F(Z)=\log\frac{Z+1-2\alpha}Z+\log\frac{Z+1+2\alpha}{Z+2}$
gives
$(e^{-4t}-1)\Upsilon_A(t)/t=\bigl[1+e^{-2t}-2e^{-t}\cosh2\alpha t\bigr]/t$, and
multiplying numerator and denominator by $e^{2t}$ yields \eqref{eq:closed}.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
(i) is $\cosh2\alpha t=\sum_k(4A)^kt^{2k}/(2k)!$ read off \eqref{eq:closed};
(ii) is $\cosh2\alpha t=\cosh t$ at $\alpha=\pm\frac12$; (iii) is
$\alpha=0$, where $\frac12(\operatorname{csch}t+\operatorname{sech}t)(1-\cosh t)
=\frac12(\operatorname{sech}t-\tanh\frac t2-1)$.  For
Corollary~\ref{cor:R}: exchanging $p$ and $q$, that is, complex
conjugation, exchanges the roles of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ in
\eqref{eq:F}, so $\overline{L_n(A,B)}=L_n(B,A)$ for real $A,B$.  Hence
$\operatorname{Re}g_n=\frac12(\partial_A+\partial_B)L_n|_{A=B=0}$, i.e.\ half the
derivative along the diagonal, so
$2\operatorname{Re}\Phi=\partial_A\Upsilon_A|_{A=0}$; and
$\partial_A\cosh2\alpha t|_{A=0}=2t^2$ gives
$\operatorname{Re}\Phi=t^2e^t/\sinh2t=\frac{t^2}2(\operatorname{csch}t
+\operatorname{sech}t)$.  Expanding
$\operatorname{sech}t=\sum_j\mathsf E_{2j}t^{2j}/(2j)!$ and
$\operatorname{csch}t=\frac1t+\sum_{k\ge1}2(1-2^{2k-1})\mathcal B_{2k}t^{2k-1}/(2k)!$
gives the coefficient formulas.  Finally Euler numbers are odd integers and, by von
Staudt--Clausen, $\nu_2(\mathcal B_{2k})=-1$ because $2-1=1$ divides $2k$; since
$1-2^{2k-1}$ is odd, $\nu_2(\operatorname{Re}g_n)=-1$ for every $n$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:genladder}
For every $\ell\ge0$ and arbitrary $p,q$,
\begin{align}
  &\text{\upshape(i)}\qquad
  \xi^2\Pi_\ell'+(\sigma-2\ell \xi)\,\Pi_\ell=\widetilde C_\ell,\label{eq:S3gen}\\
  &\text{\upshape(ii)}\qquad
  \widetilde C_{\ell+1}=\widetilde D_\ell+\rho\,(2\ell+1)\,\xi\,\Pi_\ell,\qquad
  \widetilde D_{\ell+1}=\widetilde C_\ell+2(2\ell+1)\,\xi\,\Pi_\ell,\label{eq:mixed}\\
  &\text{\upshape(iii)}\qquad
  \widetilde C_{\ell+2}=\widetilde C_\ell+2(2\ell+1)\,\xi\,\Pi_\ell
    +\rho\,(2\ell+3)\,\xi\,\Pi_{\ell+1}.\label{eq:S4gen}
\end{align}
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
(i)  Lemma~\ref{lem:bessel}(a) at $x=p\xi$ reads
$p\,\xi^2U'=(\ell p\xi-1)U+U_-$, and similarly at $x=q\xi$; hence
$\xi^2\Pi_\ell'=\bigl[(\ell p\xi-1)U+U_-\bigr]V/p+U\bigl[(\ell q\xi-1)V+V_-\bigr]/q
=(2\ell \xi-\sigma)\Pi_\ell+\widetilde C_\ell$.
(ii)  With $U_+=y_{\ell+1}(p\xi)$, $V_+=y_{\ell+1}(q\xi)$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:bessel}(b) gives $U_+=(2\ell+1)p\xi U+U_-$,
$V_+=(2\ell+1)q\xi V+V_-$, so
\[
  \widetilde C_{\ell+1}=\frac{UV_+}{p}+\frac{U_+V}{q}
  =(2\ell+1)\xi\Bigl(\frac qp+\frac pq\Bigr)UV+\frac{UV_-}{p}+\frac{U_-V}{q}
  =\rho(2\ell+1)\xi \Pi_\ell+\widetilde D_\ell,
\]
and likewise
$\widetilde D_{\ell+1}=2(2\ell+1)\xi \Pi_\ell+\widetilde C_\ell$.
(iii)  Compose the two identities of (ii).
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:curverel}
For a general angle $0<\theta<\pi$ the series \eqref{eq:F} is taken with
the weights $p=2/(1-e^{i\theta})$, $q=2/(1+e^{i\theta})$.  They satisfy
\[
  p+q=pq=\frac4{1-e^{2i\theta}}=:\varpi,
  \qquad\text{hence}\qquad
  \sigma=1,\qquad \rho=\varpi-2
\]
\emph{identically in} $\theta$, not only at the midpoint $\theta=\pi/2$ (where $\varpi=2$).
Equivalently, in the variables $x=p/2$, $y=q/2$, the weights lie on the
curve $x+y=2xy$, which we call the \emph{physical curve}; $x$ and $y$ are
the \emph{Horn variables}.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
$p+q=2\bigl[(1+e^{i\theta})+(1-e^{i\theta})\bigr]/(1-e^{2i\theta})=4/(1-e^{2i\theta})=pq$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:curvecontig}
On the physical curve, for every $\ell\ge0$, as rational functions in
$\mathbb Q(\varpi)(Z)$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:curvecontig}
  F_{\ell+2}(Z)\,(Z-2\ell-4)
  =F_\ell(Z)\,(Z+2\ell+2)+(\varpi-2)(2\ell+3)\,F_{\ell+1}(Z).
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:genladder}(i) with $\sigma=1$, comparing coefficients of
$\xi^{m+1}$, $G^{(\ell)}_{m+1}+(m-2\ell)G^{(\ell)}_m=[\xi^{m+1}]\widetilde C_{\ell}$ for
$m\ge0$; by Theorem~\ref{thm:genladder}(iii) with $\rho=\varpi-2$,
$[\xi^{m+1}]\widetilde C_{\ell+2}=[\xi^{m+1}]\widetilde C_{\ell}+2(2\ell+1)G^{(\ell)}_m
+(\varpi-2)(2\ell+3)G^{(\ell+1)}_m$.  Eliminating $\widetilde C$,
\[
  G^{(\ell+2)}_{m+1}+(m-2\ell-4)G^{(\ell+2)}_m
  =G^{(\ell)}_{m+1}+(m+2\ell+2)G^{(\ell)}_m
   +(\varpi-2)(2\ell+3)G^{(\ell+1)}_m\qquad(m\ge0),
\]
and the translation argument of Proposition~\ref{prop:Frec} (the case $m=0$
supplies the constants, and the coefficients of $Z$ agree because
$G_0^{(\ell)}=1$) yields \eqref{eq:curvecontig}.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:Prec}
For every $\ell\ge0$,
$F_\ell(Z)=P_\ell(Z;\varpi)/\bigl((Z-2)(Z-4)\cdots(Z-2\ell)\bigr)$
with $P_\ell\in\mathbb Z[\varpi][Z]$ monic of degree $\ell$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Prec}
  P_0=1,\qquad P_1=Z+\varpi-2,\qquad
  P_{\ell+2}(Z)=\bigl(Z^2-(2\ell+2)^2\bigr)P_\ell(Z)
  +(\varpi-2)(2\ell+3)\,P_{\ell+1}(Z).
\end{equation}
At $\varpi=2$ this collapses to $P_{\ell+2}=(Z^2-(2\ell+2)^2)P_\ell$, whose
solutions are the numerators of the Gamma quotient of
Theorem~\ref{thm:halfinteger}:
$S_{2m}=\prod_{j=1}^m(Z^2-(4j-2)^2)$,
$S_{2m+1}=Z\prod_{j=1}^m(Z^2-16j^2)$, so that uniformly
$S_{\nu+2}=(Z^2-(2\nu+2)^2)S_\nu$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
$\Pi_1=(1+p\xi)(1+q\xi)=1+\varpi \xi+\varpi \xi^2$ gives
$F_1=1+\varpi e_1+\varpi e_2=(Z^2+(\varpi-3)Z+2-\varpi)/((Z-1)(Z-2))=(Z+\varpi-2)/(Z-2)$,
the numerator vanishing at $Z=1$.  Solving \eqref{eq:curvecontig} for
$F_{\ell+2}$ and clearing denominators gives
$P_{\ell+2}=(Z+2\ell+2)(Z-2\ell-2)P_\ell+(\varpi-2)(2\ell+3)P_{\ell+1}$ by
induction.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:ballot}
For every $\ell\ge0$, with $d=\ell-k$ in the summand indexed by $k$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ballot}
  P_\ell(Z;2+\varpi_0)=\sum_{k=0}^{\ell}(2k-1)!!\binom{\ell+k}{2k}\varpi_0^k
  \sum_{j\ge0}(-1)^j\,\frac{d!}{(d-2j)!}\;\mathfrak b_j(k)\,S_{d-2j}(Z),
\end{equation}
the inner sum running over $j\le d/2$.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
The proof consists in verifying that the closed coefficients
\eqref{eq:ballot} satisfy the same recurrence and the same initial data
as the curve numerators: the interior identity is checked first, then
the boundary patterns excluded by the interior divisions, then the base
cases; induction closes the argument.
The polynomials $S_\nu$ have degree $\nu$, so the expansion of any polynomial in
the basis $\{\varpi_0^kS_\nu\}$ is unique.  Write
$c(\ell,k,j)=(2k-1)!!\binom{\ell+k}{2k}(-1)^j\frac{d!}{(d-2j)!}\mathfrak b_j(k)$
for the coefficient of $\varpi_0^kS_{\ell-k-2j}$ in \eqref{eq:ballot}, with
$c(\ell,k,j)=0$ outside $0\le k\le\ell$, $0\le2j\le d$.  Since
$Z^2S_\nu=S_{\nu+2}+(2\nu+2)^2S_\nu$, substituting \eqref{eq:ballot} into
\eqref{eq:Prec} and matching the coefficient of $\varpi_0^kS_\nu$ with
$\nu=(\ell+2)-k-2J$ reduces the claim, by uniqueness, to the four-term
identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fourterm}
  c(\ell+2,k,J)=c(\ell,k,J)-4(k+2J-2)(2\ell+4-k-2J)\,c(\ell,k,J-1)
  +(2\ell+3)\,c(\ell+1,k-1,J).
\end{equation}
We verify \eqref{eq:fourterm} for all indices, including the boundary
patterns.  First suppose $k\ge1$.  The coefficient admits the factorial form
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cfactorial}
 c(\ell,k,j)
 =(-1)^j
 \frac{(\ell+k)!\,(2j+k-1)!}
 {2^k(k-1)!\,j!\,(j+k)!\,(\ell-k-2j)!},
\end{equation}
whenever $\ell-k-2j\ge0$; outside this range it is zero by convention.
This follows immediately from
$(2k-1)!!=(2k)!/(2^kk!)$ and
$\mathfrak b_j(k)=k(2j+k-1)!/(j!(j+k)!)$.

For the interior range $J\ge1$ and $n:=\ell-k-2J\ge0$, division by the
nonzero coefficient $c(\ell,k,J)$ gives
\[
  \frac{c(\ell+2,k,J)}{c(\ell,k,J)}
  =\frac{(\ell+k+1)(\ell+k+2)}{(n+1)(n+2)},
\]
\[
  \frac{c(\ell+1,k-1,J)}{c(\ell,k,J)}
  =\frac{2(k-1)(J+k)}{(n+1)(n+2)(2J+k-1)},
\]
\[
  \frac{c(\ell,k,J-1)}{c(\ell,k,J)}
  =\frac{-\,J(J+k)}
  {(n+1)(n+2)(2J+k-2)(2J+k-1)}.
\]
Substitution in \eqref{eq:fourterm}, followed by clearing denominators,
reduces the recurrence to
\begin{align}\label{eq:cubic}
  (\ell+k+1)(\ell+k+2)(2J+k-1)
  ={}&(n+1)(n+2)(2J+k-1)\notag\\
  &+4J(J+k)(2\ell+4-k-2J)\notag\\
  &+2(2\ell+3)(k-1)(J+k),
\end{align}
and after $\ell=n+k+2J$ both sides expand to the same cubic polynomial.

It remains to treat the boundary cases excluded by that division.  If $k=0$, then
$c(\ell,0,0)=1$ and $c(\ell,0,j)=0$ for $j\ge1$.  Hence
\eqref{eq:fourterm} is immediate: for $J=0$ it is $1=1$, for $J=1$ the only
potential term $c(\ell,0,0)$ is multiplied by
$k+2J-2=0$, and for $J\ge2$ every term is zero.

Now let $k\ge1$ and $J=0$.  If $k\le\ell$, the middle term of
\eqref{eq:fourterm} vanishes and \eqref{eq:cfactorial} gives
\[
 \frac{c(\ell+2,k,0)}{c(\ell,k,0)}
 =\frac{(\ell+k+1)(\ell+k+2)}
        {(\ell-k+1)(\ell-k+2)},\qquad
 \frac{c(\ell+1,k-1,0)}{c(\ell,k,0)}
 =\frac{2k}{(\ell-k+1)(\ell-k+2)}.
\]
(For $k=1$ one uses $c(\ell+1,0,0)=1$ directly.)  Their substitution gives
$c(\ell+2,k,0)=c(\ell,k,0)+(2\ell+3)c(\ell+1,k-1,0)$ exactly.  The only
remaining $J=0$ targets have $k=\ell+1$ or $k=\ell+2$; then
$c(\ell,k,0)=0$ and the middle term is again zero, while direct evaluation
of the double-factorial formula gives
\[
 c(\ell+2,k,0)=(2\ell+3)c(\ell+1,k-1,0)=(2\ell+3)!!.
\]

Finally take $J\ge1$.  When the target coefficient
$c(\ell+2,k,J)$ exists but $c(\ell,k,J)$ does not, necessarily
$n=-2$ or $n=-1$; these are the only remaining possibilities because the
target basis index is $n+2\ge0$.  For $n=-2$,
\[
 \frac{c(\ell,k,J-1)}{c(\ell+2,k,J)}
 =-\frac{J}
 {2(2J+k-2)(2J+k-1)(2J+2k-1)},
\]
\[
 \frac{c(\ell+1,k-1,J)}{c(\ell+2,k,J)}
 =\frac{k-1}{(2J+k-1)(2J+2k-1)}.
\]
Since here $\ell=k+2J-2$, insertion in the right-hand side of
\eqref{eq:fourterm} gives exactly $1$ after division by
$c(\ell+2,k,J)$.  For $n=-1$ the corresponding ratios are
\[
 \frac{c(\ell,k,J-1)}{c(\ell+2,k,J)}
 =-\frac{J}
 {2(2J+k-2)(2J+k-1)(2J+2k+1)},
\]
\[
 \frac{c(\ell+1,k-1,J)}{c(\ell+2,k,J)}
 =\frac{k-1}{(2J+k-1)(2J+2k+1)},
\]
and with $\ell=k+2J-1$ the same substitution again gives $1$.  These formulas
also cover $k=1$, because then
$c(\ell+1,0,J)=0$ for $J\ge1$ and the factor $k-1$ vanishes.  Thus
\eqref{eq:fourterm} holds for every admissible coefficient.

With the base cases $P_0=1=c(0,0,0)S_0$ and
$P_1=Z+\varpi_0=S_1+\varpi_0S_0$, induction on $\ell$ through \eqref{eq:Prec} completes
the proof.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:offcurve}
The curve $\sigma=1$ passes through the midpoint in the plane of the
Horn variables $(x,y)$.  On it, Theorem~\ref{thm:curvecontig}, the
degree bound of Lemma~\ref{lem:degree} (valid at any fixed $(x,y)$) and
interpolation at $A=(\ell+\frac12)^2$ determine the diagonal amplitude
for all $\alpha$.  The derivatives normal to the curve are not
determined in this way: for $\sigma\ne1$ the coefficient relations take
the form $\sigma G_{m+1}+(m-c)G_m$, and their translation to the basis
$e_m$ involves, in addition, the operation
$\sum_mG_me_m\mapsto\sum_mmG_me_m$, which is not expressible through
rational operations and shifts in $Z$.  This operation is studied in
Section~\ref{sec:indexop}.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- definitionx-2: body_md -->
On an inverse-factorial series define the \emph{index operator}
\[
 \mathcal I\Bigl(\sum_{m\ge0}G_me_m\Bigr)=\sum_{m\ge0}mG_me_m.
\]
<!-- end definitionx-2 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:Mclosure}
If every $G_m(x,y)$ is homogeneous of total degree $m$, then
$\mathcal IF=(\Theta_x+\Theta_y)F$, where $\Theta_x=x\partial_x$ and
$\Theta_y=y\partial_y$.
Moreover, if $G_0=1$ and
$\mathcal RF=\sum_{m\ge0}G_{m+1}e_m$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Rclosure}
 \mathcal RF=Z(F-1)-\mathcal IF,
\end{equation}
and if $F$ is symmetric in $p,q$, hence a function of $(\sigma,\rho)$,
then at fixed $\rho$, $\mathcal I=-\sigma\partial_\sigma$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Homogeneity gives the first assertion.  Lemma~\ref{lem:basis} gives
$ZF=Z+\sum_{m\ge1}G_me_{m-1}+\sum_{m\ge1}mG_me_m
=Z+\mathcal RF+\mathcal IF$, which is \eqref{eq:Rclosure}.  Under a common
scaling $(p,q)\mapsto(rp,rq)$, $\rho$ is fixed and
$\sigma\mapsto r^{-1}\sigma$; hence $\Theta_x+\Theta_y=-\sigma\partial_\sigma$
at fixed $\rho$.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:Mladder}
For every $\ell\ge0$ and arbitrary $(\sigma,\rho)$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Mladder}
 \mathcal Q_{2\ell+4}^{(\sigma)}F_{\ell+2}
 =\mathcal Q_{-2\ell-2}^{(\sigma)}F_\ell
  +\rho(2\ell+3)F_{\ell+1}.
\end{equation}
At $\sigma=1$ this reduces to the curve contiguity
\eqref{eq:curvecontig}.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
From Theorem~\ref{thm:genladder}(i), comparison of the coefficient of
$\xi^{m+1}$ gives
$\sigma G_{m+1}^{(\ell)}+(m-2\ell)G_m^{(\ell)}=[\xi^{m+1}]\widetilde C_\ell$.
Use Theorem~\ref{thm:genladder}(iii) to eliminate $\widetilde C_{\ell+2}$ and
$\widetilde C_\ell$.  One obtains, for every $m\ge0$,
\begin{align*}
 \sigma G_{m+1}^{(\ell+2)}+(m-2\ell-4)G_m^{(\ell+2)}
 ={}&\sigma G_{m+1}^{(\ell)}+(m+2\ell+2)G_m^{(\ell)}
 +\rho(2\ell+3)G_m^{(\ell+1)}.
\end{align*}
Multiplication by $e_m$ and summation give
\eqref{eq:Mladder}.  At $\sigma=1$, \eqref{eq:Qoperator} becomes
$\mathcal Q_c^{(1)}F=(Z-c)F-Z$; the two copies of $-Z$ cancel and
\eqref{eq:curvecontig} follows.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:normaljets}
Put
$F_{\ell}^{[k]}(Z;\rho)
=\partial_\sigma^kF_\ell(Z;\sigma,\rho)\big|_{\sigma=1}$ for $k\ge0$,
with $F_{\ell}^{[-1]}=0$.  Then
\begin{align}\label{eq:jetladder}
 &(Z+k-2\ell-4)F_{\ell+2}^{[k]}
   +k(Z+k-1)F_{\ell+2}^{[k-1]}\notag\\
 &\qquad=(Z+k+2\ell+2)F_{\ell}^{[k]}
   +k(Z+k-1)F_{\ell}^{[k-1]}
   +\rho(2\ell+3)F_{\ell+1}^{[k]}.
\end{align}
In particular, at the midpoint $\rho=0$, the two parity ladders decouple
and every $F_\ell^{[k]}$ is obtained recursively from the two base families
$F_0$ and $F_1$.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
For $k\ge1$, Leibniz' rule applied to \eqref{eq:Qoperator} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Qjet}
 \partial_\sigma^k\mathcal Q_c^{(\sigma)}F\big|_{\sigma=1}
 =(Z+k-c)F^{[k]}+k(Z+k-1)F^{[k-1]}-\delta_{k,1}Z:
\end{equation}
only the first two derivatives of $\sigma(1-\sigma)$ are nonzero, and
their contributions combine with the derivative of $\sigma Z(F-1)$ exactly
as displayed.  For $k=0$ the formula is
$\mathcal Q_c^{(1)}F=(Z-c)F^{[0]}-Z$.  For $k\le1$ the terms $-Z$,
which do not depend on $c$, cancel between the two
sides of \eqref{eq:Mladder}.  Differentiating \eqref{eq:Mladder} $k$ times
and using \eqref{eq:Qjet} proves \eqref{eq:jetladder}.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:indexop}
For each fixed order in $Z^{-1}$ and each fixed $k$, the interpolation
argument of Section~\ref{sec:transfer} extends \eqref{eq:jetladder},
written with $2\ell+1=2\alpha$ and with $F_\ell,F_{\ell+1},F_{\ell+2}$
replaced by the diagonal amplitudes at $\alpha,\alpha+1,\alpha+2$, from
$\alpha=\ell+\tfrac12$ to arbitrary $\alpha$, each coefficient being a
polynomial in $\alpha$.  Thus the diagonal
amplitude is formally determined, to any prescribed order in
$\sigma-1$, in a neighbourhood of the physical curve.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:twopar}
For all $\ell,m\ge0$, at the midpoint,
\begin{align}
 &\xi^2\Pi_{\ell,m}'+\bigl(1-(\ell+m)\xi\bigr)\Pi_{\ell,m}=\widetilde C_{\ell,m}, \label{eq:2parS3}\\
&\widetilde C_{\ell+1,m+1}=\widetilde D_{\ell,m}+2i(\ell-m)\,\xi\,\Pi_{\ell,m},\qquad  \widetilde D_{\ell+1,m+1}=\widetilde C_{\ell,m}+2(\ell+m+1)\,\xi\,\Pi_{\ell,m},  \label{eq:2parmixed}\\
 &F_{\ell+2,m+2}(Z)\,\bigl(Z-(\ell+m)-4\bigr) \label{eq:2parcontig} \\
 &\qquad =F_{\ell,m}(Z)\,\bigl(Z+(\ell+m)+2\bigr)+2i(\ell-m)\,F_{\ell+1,m+1}(Z).   \nonumber
 \end{align}
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
\eqref{eq:2parS3} is the computation of Theorem~\ref{thm:genladder}(i) with the two
orders kept distinct, using $\sigma=1$.  For \eqref{eq:2parmixed}, with $U=y_\ell(p\xi)$,
$V=y_m(q\xi)$,
\[
  \widetilde C_{\ell+1,m+1}=\frac{UV_+}{p}+\frac{U_+V}{q}
  =\xi\Bigl[(2m+1)\frac qp+(2\ell+1)\frac pq\Bigr]\Pi_{\ell,m}+\widetilde D_{\ell,m},
\]
and at the midpoint $q/p=-i$, $p/q=i$, so the bracket is $2i(\ell-m)$; the
second identity has bracket $(2\ell+1)+(2m+1)$.  Composing gives
$\widetilde C_{\ell+2,m+2}=\widetilde C_{\ell,m}+2(\ell+m+1)\xi \Pi_{\ell,m}
+2i(\ell-m)\xi \Pi_{\ell+1,m+1}$, and the translation of
Theorem~\ref{thm:curvecontig}, with $\ell+m$ in place of $2\ell$, yields
\eqref{eq:2parcontig}; the constants match because
$G^{(\ell,m)}_1=\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}2p+\frac{m(m+1)}2q$ gives
$G^{(\ell+2,m+2)}_1-G^{(\ell,m)}_1
=\bigl[(\ell+m)+2\bigr]+\bigl[(\ell+m)+4\bigr]+2i(\ell-m)$.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:KdF}
For every $\ell\ge0$,
$F_{\ell,0}(Z)=\operatorname{{}_2F_1}\bigl(-\ell,\ell+1;1-Z;x_0\bigr)$ with
$x_0=\frac{1+i}2$.  More generally, for all $\alpha,\beta$, as formal
series,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:KdF}
  F(\alpha,\beta;Z)=\sum_{\mu,\nu\ge0}
  \frac{(\tfrac12-\alpha)_\mu(\tfrac12+\alpha)_\mu
        (\tfrac12-\beta)_\nu(\tfrac12+\beta)_\nu}
       {(1-Z)_{\mu+\nu}\;\mu!\,\nu!}\;x_0^{\,\mu}y_0^{\,\nu},
\end{equation}
a Kamp\'e de F\'eriet function $F^{0:2;2}_{1:0;0}$ at arguments with
$x_0+y_0=1$, $x_0y_0=\frac12$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
$e_n(Z)=(-1)^n/(1-Z)_n$ and
$a_\mu(\alpha)(2x_0)^\mu(-1)^\mu
=(\tfrac12-\alpha)_\mu(\tfrac12+\alpha)_\mu x_0^\mu/\mu!$, term by term in
\eqref{eq:F}.  At $\alpha=\ell+\frac12$, $\beta=\frac12$, only $\nu=0$
survives and the $\mu$-series terminates.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:appellreduce}
Put $c=1-Z$, $b_1=\frac12+\alpha$, $b_2=\frac12+\beta$.  On
\[
       y=\frac{x}{2x-1},
       \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad x+y=2xy,
\]
one has, for generic parameters and then by meromorphic continuation,
\begin{align}
 \mathcal F\!\left(\alpha,\beta;Z;x,\frac{x}{2x-1}\right)
  ={}&(1-x)^{c-1}(1-2x)^{b_2}\notag\\
 &\times {}_2F_1\!\left(
  \frac{b_2-b_1+c}{2},
  \frac{b_1+b_2+c-1}{2};c;4x(1-x)\right).
 \label{eq:appellreduce}
\end{align}
The branches are those obtained by analytic continuation from a neighbourhood
of $x=0$ along the chosen path.
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
The four upper parameters of our $F_3$ are
$1-b_1,1-b_2;b_1,b_2$.  The fourth pair in Theorem~3.1 of
Vid\=unas~\cite{VidunasAppell} is therefore exactly the pair displayed in
\eqref{eq:appellreduce}.  Immediately after that theorem, Vid\=unas states
that in the first and fourth pairs the two functions are directly identical
in a neighbourhood of $x=0$ (not merely solutions of the same second-order
ODE).  Hence \eqref{eq:appellreduce} holds on the common germ at $x=0$.
The relation $y=x/(2x-1)$ is the physical-curve identity already used in
Section~\ref{sec:curve}.  Therefore the two sides represent the same analytic
germ near $x=0$.  Analytic continuation of this common germ along any path
avoiding the singular locus gives the stated identity.  Notice that this is
an identity for fixed generic $Z$ (and then meromorphically in the
parameters); no passage to the large-$Z$ limit is used in establishing it.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:gausstangent}
Set $s=(1-Z)/2$ and
\[
 \mathcal H(\alpha;Z)
 ={}_2F_1^{\uparrow}\!\left(s-\frac\alpha2,
                                  s+\frac\alpha2;2s;2\right).
\]
Then the inverse-power expansion at $Z=\infty$ inherited coefficientwise
from the defining inverse-factorial series for $F$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gausstangent}
 \sum_{n\ge1}g_n Z^{-n}
 =\frac12\left.\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\alpha^2}
       \log\mathcal H(\alpha;Z)\right|_{\alpha=0}
 =\frac12\,\frac{\partial_\alpha^2\mathcal H(0;Z)}{\mathcal H(0;Z)}.
\end{equation}
The last expression is independent of a choice of logarithm.  In particular
the two numerator parameters in \eqref{eq:gausstangent} sum to the
denominator parameter: the series $\sum_ng_nZ^{-n}$ is obtained from a
parameter variation of a single \emph{zero-balanced} Gauss function.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Take $\beta=0$ in \eqref{eq:midpoint2F1}.  Its prefactor is independent of
$\alpha$.  Since $A=\alpha^2$ and the left-hand side is even in $\alpha$,
$\partial_A|_{A=0}=\frac12\partial_\alpha^2|_{\alpha=0}$.  The function
$\mathcal H$ is itself even in $\alpha$, so $\partial_\alpha\mathcal H(0;Z)=0$;
therefore the second logarithmic derivative is
$\partial_\alpha^2\mathcal H(0;Z)/\mathcal H(0;Z)$.  Finally, $F=1+O(Z^{-1})$ coefficientwise, so its formal logarithm at
$Z=\infty$ is uniquely defined.  Since \eqref{eq:midpoint2F1} is an exact
identity for generic fixed $Z$, the formal inverse-power expansion used in
this paper may be taken on either side; the coefficients inherited from the
left-hand inverse-factorial series are therefore exactly those in
\eqref{eq:gausstangent}.  No assertion about convergence of the resulting
$Z^{-1}$ series is needed.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rem:nodes}
$\kappa_r$ is a polynomial in $(A,B)$; its values on the grid
$A_\ell=(\ell+\frac12)^2$, $B_m=(m+\frac12)^2$ are determined by the
rational functions $F_{\ell,m}$, and the node differences
$A_\ell-A_m=(\ell-m)(\ell+m+1)$ are integers.  The recurrence
\eqref{eq:2parcontig} therefore expresses $[A^1B^0]\kappa_r$ as a
Lagrange interpolation functional with integer node differences.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:quadeval}
\[
 \mathcal H(0;Z)={}_2F_1^{\uparrow}(s,s;2s;2)
 =e^{i\pi s/2}\,\frac{\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma(s+\frac12)}{\Gamma(\frac{s+1}2)^2}.
\]
In particular
$\operatorname{Im}\mathcal H(0;Z)/\operatorname{Re}\mathcal H(0;Z)
=\tan\frac{\pi s}2$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
The quadratic transformation \cite[Sec.~3.1]{AndrewsAskeyRoy}
\[
 {}_2F_1(a,b;2b;z)
 =(1-z)^{-a/2}\,{}_2F_1\Bigl(\frac a2,\,b-\frac a2;\,b+\frac12;\,
 \frac{z^2}{4(z-1)}\Bigr)
\]
at $a=b=s$ has transformed argument
$z^2/(4(z-1))\to1$ as $z\to2$, and the right-hand Gauss series is
continuous up to argument $1$ because there
$\operatorname{Re}(c-a-b)=\frac12>0$; Gauss's summation gives
${}_2F_1(\frac s2,\frac s2;s+\frac12;1)
=\Gamma(s+\frac12)\Gamma(\frac12)/\Gamma(\frac{s+1}2)^2$.
Approaching from $\operatorname{Im}z>0$, $\log(1-z)\to-i\pi$, so
$(1-z)^{-s/2}\to e^{i\pi s/2}$.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:split}
For $\operatorname{Re}s<\frac12$ and $2s\notin\mathbb Z$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:split}
 \mathcal H(\alpha;Z)
 =\frac{\Gamma(2s)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}
 \bigl[\mathsf S(\alpha;s)+i\pi\,\mathsf K(\alpha;s)\bigr],
\end{equation}
where
\[
 \mathsf K(\alpha;s)={}_2F_1(a,b;1;-1),\qquad
 \mathsf S(\alpha;s)=\sum_{n\ge0}(-1)^n\frac{(a)_n(b)_n}{(n!)^2}
 \bigl[2\psi(n+1)-\psi(a+n)-\psi(b+n)\bigr],
\]
both series converging absolutely.  In particular, for real $\alpha$ the
imaginary part of the boundary value is
$\pi\Gamma(2s)\,{}_2F_1(a,b;1;-1)/(\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b))$.
At the Legendre point $\alpha=0$ both blocks have closed forms:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:blocksclosed}
 \mathsf K(0;s)=\frac{\Gamma(1+\frac s2)}{\Gamma(1+s)\,\Gamma(1-\frac s2)}
 \quad\text{\emph{(Kummer)}},\qquad
 \mathsf S(0;s)=\cos\frac{\pi s}2\cdot
 \frac{\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma(s+\frac12)\,\Gamma(s)^2}
      {\Gamma(2s)\,\Gamma(\frac{s+1}2)^2}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Write $R_n(a,b)=2\psi(n+1)-\psi(a+n)-\psi(b+n)$.  The zero-balanced
connection formula
\cite[Sec.~2.3]{AndrewsAskeyRoy} (see also \cite[Eq.~15.8.10]{DLMF})
gives, for $|1-z|<1$,
$|\arg(1-z)|<\pi$,
\[
 {}_2F_1(a,b;a+b;z)
 =\frac{\Gamma(a+b)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}
 \sum_{n\ge0}\frac{(a)_n(b)_n}{(n!)^2}
 \bigl[R_n(a,b)-\log(1-z)\bigr](1-z)^n .
\]
On the upper approach $z\to2+i0$ one has $1-z\to-1-i0$, so
$\log(1-z)\to-i\pi$ and $(1-z)^n\to(-1)^n$; the two limiting series are
absolutely convergent for $\operatorname{Re}(a+b)<1$ since their terms are
$O(n^{\operatorname{Re}(a+b)-2}\log n)$, and the boundary value is attained
by Abel continuity along the path.  The digamma-free part is the Taylor
series of ${}_2F_1(a,b;1;-1)$ because $(1)_n=n!$.  The first evaluation
in \eqref{eq:blocksclosed} is Kummer's theorem
${}_2F_1(a,b;1+a-b;-1)$ at $a=b=s$; the second follows from
Lemma~\ref{lem:quadeval} by taking real parts in \eqref{eq:split}.
The $n=0$ kernel $2\psi(1)-\psi(a)-\psi(b)$ is precisely the constant
$R(a,b)=-2\gamma-\psi(a)-\psi(b)$ governing the zero-balanced asymptotics
studied in \cite{AndersonEtAl,SimicVuorinen}.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:Kcontig}
For all $\alpha$ and generic $s$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Kcontig}
 4(s-1)(4s^2-\alpha^2)\,\mathsf K(\alpha;s+1)
 +2\alpha^2(2s-1)\,\mathsf K(\alpha;s)
 +s\bigl(4(s-1)^2-\alpha^2\bigr)\,\mathsf K(\alpha;s-1)=0 .
\end{equation}
At $\alpha=0$ this degenerates to the two-term relation
$4s\,\mathsf K(0;s+1)+(s-1)\,\mathsf K(0;s-1)=0$, which is also satisfied by
the closed form of $\mathsf K(0;s)$ in \eqref{eq:blocksclosed}.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Assume first that $\operatorname{Re}s<-\frac12$, so that the three
series converge absolutely.  With $t_n=(-1)^n(a)_n(b)_n/(n!)^2$, the shifted
series have termwise ratios
$t_n^{+}=t_n(a+n)(b+n)/(ab)$ and $t_n^{-}=t_n(a-1)(b-1)/((a-1+n)(b-1+n))$,
and the rational function
\begin{gather*}
 r(n)=\frac{-n^2\,\mathsf P(n)}{(a-1+n)(b-1+n)},\\
 \mathsf P(n)=8(s-1)n^2+8(3s-2)(s-1)n+4(5s-2)(s-1)^2+(2-s)\alpha^2,
\end{gather*}
satisfies the identity
\[
 c_+\,\frac{(a+n)(b+n)}{ab}+c_0
 +c_-\,\frac{(a-1)(b-1)}{(a-1+n)(b-1+n)}
 =-\frac{(a+n)(b+n)}{(n+1)^2}\,r(n+1)-r(n)
\]
where $c_+,c_0,c_-$ denote the three coefficients of \eqref{eq:Kcontig}, in
this order (an identity of rational functions of $(n,s,\alpha)$).
Multiplying by $t_n$ and summing over $n\ge0$, the right side telescopes:
$r(0)=0$, and $t_nr(n)=O(n^{2\operatorname{Re}s})\to0$.  This proves
\eqref{eq:Kcontig} for $\operatorname{Re}s<-\frac12$, and the general
case follows by analytic continuation in $s$, since
${}_2F_1(a,b;1;-1)$ is an entire function of $a$ and $b$.  The $\alpha=0$
degeneration follows since the middle coefficient carries $\alpha^2$;
that the closed form of $\mathsf K(0;s)$ satisfies it is the elementary computation
$\mathsf K(0;s+1)/\mathsf K(0;s-1)=-(s-1)/(4s)$.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:quad}
Let
\[
 \mathsf K_2(s):=\partial_\alpha^2\mathsf K(\alpha;s)\big|_{\alpha=0}
 =-\frac12\sum_{n\ge1}(-1)^n\Bigl(\frac{(s)_n}{n!}\Bigr)^{\!2}
 \sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac1{(s+j)^2},
\]
a series with rational terms.  Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $\mathsf K_2$ satisfies the inhomogeneous two-term recurrence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:K2rec}
 8s^2(s-1)\,\mathsf K_2(s+1)+2s(s-1)^2\,\mathsf K_2(s-1)
 =4(s-1)\,\mathsf K_0(s+1)-2(2s-1)\,\mathsf K_0(s)+s\,\mathsf K_0(s-1),
\end{equation}
with $\mathsf K_0=\mathsf K(0;\cdot)$.
Equivalently, the normalised quotient
$Q=\mathsf K_2/\mathsf K_0$ obeys the exact difference equation
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Qdiff}
 Q(s+1)-Q(s-1)=\mathsf f(s),\qquad
 \mathsf f(s)=-\frac{2s-1}{2s^2(s-1)^2}
 -\frac{(2s-1)\,\mathsf r(s)}{4s^2(s-1)},
\end{equation}
where
$\mathsf r(s)=\mathsf K_0(s)/\mathsf K_0(s+1)
=2\,\Gamma(1+\frac s2)\Gamma(\frac{1-s}2)\big/
 \bigl(\Gamma(1-\frac s2)\Gamma(\frac{1+s}2)\bigr)$.
\item[(ii)] On each lattice $\{s_0-2k\}_{k\ge0}$, $\mathsf r$ is bounded
and $\mathsf f(\varsigma)=O(\varsigma^{-2})$, so
$\sum_{k\ge0}\mathsf f(s-1-2k)$ converges absolutely and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadrature}
 \mathsf K_2(s)=\mathsf K_0(s)
 \Bigl[c_*(s_0)+\sum_{k\ge0}\mathsf f(s-1-2k)\Bigr]
\end{equation}
with a constant $c_*(s_0)$ depending only on the lattice.  This constant
is in fact zero (Theorem~\ref{thm:czero}).
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Since $(a)_n(b)_n=\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\bigl((s+j)^2-\alpha^2/4\bigr)$,
one has
\[
 \partial_\alpha^2\bigl[(a)_n(b)_n\bigr]_{\alpha=0}
 =-\frac12(s)_n^2\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac1{(s+j)^2},
\]
which gives the series for $\mathsf K_2$.  (i)~Differentiate \eqref{eq:Kcontig} twice at $\alpha=0$: the
first $\alpha$-derivatives vanish by evenness, and the $\alpha^2$-parts of
the three coefficients contribute
$-8(s-1)$, $4(2s-1)$, $-2s$ against $\mathsf K_0$, giving
\eqref{eq:K2rec} after division by $2$.  Dividing \eqref{eq:K2rec} by
$8s^2(s-1)\mathsf K_0(s+1)$ and eliminating $\mathsf K_0(s-1)$ through
the two-term relation of Lemma~\ref{lem:Kcontig} yields \eqref{eq:Qdiff}.
(ii)~By reflection and Stirling,
$\Gamma(\frac{1-s}2)/\Gamma(1-\frac s2)\sim(|s|/2)^{-1/2}$ while the
quotient of the two left-hand Gammas is
$O(|s|^{1/2})$ times a trigonometric factor that is periodic on the
lattice, so $\mathsf r$ is bounded there; summing \eqref{eq:Qdiff} in
steps of two telescopes to \eqref{eq:quadrature}, the general solution of
the homogeneous equation on a fixed lattice being
$\mathsf K_0\times\mathrm{const}$.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{cor:onefun}
Fix real $Z>1$ with $s=(1-Z)/2$ generic, and let
\[
 \mathcal A(s)=\frac12\,\frac{\partial_\alpha^2\mathcal H(0;Z)}{\mathcal H(0;Z)}
\]
be the function on the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:gausstangent}.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:onefun}
 \operatorname{Im}\mathcal A
 =\frac{\pi\,\mathsf K_2(s)}{2\,\mathsf S(0;s)}
 -\tan\frac{\pi s}2
 \Bigl(\operatorname{Re}\mathcal A+\frac{\psi'(s)}4\Bigr).
\end{equation}
Every term on the right except $\mathsf K_2$ and
$\operatorname{Re}\mathcal A$ is in closed form ($\mathsf S(0;s)$ by
\eqref{eq:blocksclosed}).
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Write $\mathcal H=\mathsf G\,(\mathsf S+i\pi\mathsf K)$ with
$\mathsf G=\Gamma(2s)/(\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b))$, by
Proposition~\ref{prop:split}.  All three factors are even in $\alpha$, so
first $\alpha$-derivatives vanish at $0$ and
$2\,\mathcal A=\partial_\alpha^2\log\mathcal H|_0
=\partial_\alpha^2\log\mathsf G|_0
+\bigl(\mathsf S_2+i\pi\mathsf K_2\bigr)/\bigl(\mathsf S_0+i\pi\mathsf
K_0\bigr)$, where $\mathsf S_2,\mathsf K_2$ are the second
$\alpha$-derivatives and $\mathsf S_0,\mathsf K_0$ the values.  Since
$\partial_\alpha^2\log\mathsf G|_0=-\frac12\psi'(s)$ is real, taking real
and imaginary parts and using
$\pi\mathsf K_0/\mathsf S_0
=\operatorname{Im}\mathcal H(0)/\operatorname{Re}\mathcal H(0)
=\tan\frac{\pi s}2$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:quadeval}) to eliminate
$\mathsf S_2$ between the two resulting equations gives
\eqref{eq:onefun}.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:forcing-split}
The forcing in \eqref{eq:Qdiff} splits as
\[
 \mathsf f=\mathsf f_{\rm rat}+\mathsf f_{\Gamma},\qquad
 \mathsf f_{\rm rat}(s)=\frac1{2s^2}-\frac1{2(s-1)^2},
 \qquad
 \mathsf f_{\Gamma}(s)=-\frac{(2s-1)\,\mathsf r(s)}{4s^2(s-1)}.
\]
Moreover the Gamma quotient obeys the multiplicative step-two identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rstep}
 \mathsf r(s)\,\mathsf r(s-1)=-\frac{4s}{s-1}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
The partial-fraction identity
$\frac1{2s^2}-\frac1{2(s-1)^2}=-\frac{2s-1}{2s^2(s-1)^2}$ is immediate.
Since $\mathsf r(s)=\mathsf K_0(s)/\mathsf K_0(s+1)$, the two-term relation
$4s\,\mathsf K_0(s+1)+(s-1)\mathsf K_0(s-1)=0$ of
Lemma~\ref{lem:Kcontig} gives \eqref{eq:rstep}.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:formal-sinh}
Let $\mathbb K$ be a field of characteristic zero and let
$f(s)\in s^{-2}\mathbb K[[s^{-1}]]$.  There is a unique
$Q(s)\in s^{-1}\mathbb K[[s^{-1}]]$ satisfying
$Q(s+1)-Q(s-1)=f(s)$.  If $\partial_s^{-1}$ denotes the primitive with
zero constant term in $s^{-1}\mathbb K[[s^{-1}]]$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:formal-sinh}
 Q=\frac1{2\sinh\partial_s}f
 =\frac12\partial_s^{-1}f+
 \sum_{j\ge1}\frac{(1-2^{2j-1})\mathcal B_{2j}}{(2j)!}\,\partial_s^{2j-1}f.
\end{equation}
In particular \eqref{eq:formal-sinh} applies to $\mathsf f_{\rm rat}$; to
apply it to $\mathsf f_\Gamma$ one must first separate the
lattice-periodic factor of $\mathsf r$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:rhat} below).
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
On formal Laurent series, the central difference is
$e^{\partial_s}-e^{-\partial_s}=2\sinh\partial_s$.  Since
\[
 \frac{x}{\sinh x}=\sum_{j\ge0}
 \frac{2(1-2^{2j-1})\mathcal B_{2j}}{(2j)!}x^{2j},
\]
its inverse on series with no constant term is \eqref{eq:formal-sinh}.
The leading operator is $\partial_s$, which is bijective from
$s^{-1}\mathbb K[[s^{-1}]]$ to $s^{-2}\mathbb K[[s^{-1}]]$; this also proves
existence and uniqueness.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{cor:rational-quadrature}
The unique formal solution of
\[
 Q_{\rm rat}(s+1)-Q_{\rm rat}(s-1)=\mathsf f_{\rm rat}(s),
 \qquad Q_{\rm rat}(s)\in s^{-1}\mathbb Q[[s^{-1}]],
\]
is also the distinguished analytic solution which tends to zero along a
leftward step-two lattice.  It has the closed form
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Qrat}
 Q_{\rm rat}(s)=\frac18\left[
 \psi'\!\left(\frac{1-s}{2}\right)
 -\psi'\!\left(1-\frac s2\right)\right].
\end{equation}
Equivalently,
$Q_{\rm rat}(s)=\sum_{k\ge0}\mathsf f_{\rm rat}(s-1-2k)$,
the series converging whenever the lattice avoids the poles.
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
From $\mathsf f_{\rm rat}(\varsigma)=\frac12(\varsigma^{-2}-(\varsigma-1)^{-2})$
and $\sum_{k\ge0}(a+2k)^{-2}=\frac14\psi'(a/2)$, the lattice sum is
$\frac12\cdot\frac14[\psi'(\frac{1-s}2)-\psi'(1-\frac s2)]$, which is
\eqref{eq:Qrat}.  Alternatively, the trigamma recurrence
$\psi'(z+1)=\psi'(z)-z^{-2}$ shows directly that the central difference of
\eqref{eq:Qrat} is $\mathsf f_{\rm rat}$.  Its asymptotic expansion has no
constant term, so uniqueness follows from
Proposition~\ref{prop:formal-sinh}.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:periodic-kernel}
On functions, the kernel of the central-difference operator contains
all $2$-periodic functions; the constant $c_*(s_0)$ in
\eqref{eq:quadrature} reflects this ambiguity.  On formal series in
$s^{-1}\mathbb K[[s^{-1}]]$ the kernel is zero.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:rhat}
Put
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rhatdef}
 \widehat{\mathsf r}(s)
 :=s\left[\frac{\Gamma(s/2)}
 {\Gamma((1+s)/2)}\right]^2.
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rhatfactor}
 \mathsf r(s)=\tan\frac{\pi s}{2}\,\widehat{\mathsf r}(s).
\end{equation}
Moreover $\widehat{\mathsf r}$ has a canonical Poincar\'e expansion
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rhatformal}
 \widehat{\mathsf r}(s)\sim
 2\exp\left(
 2\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{(-1)^{n+1}
 \bigl[\mathcal B_{n+1}(0)-\mathcal B_{n+1}(\tfrac12)\bigr]}{n(n+1)}
 \left(\frac{2}{s}\right)^{\!n}\right)
 \in 2+s^{-1}\mathbb Q[[s^{-1}]].
\end{equation}
Thus every non-formal dependence of $\mathsf r$ on the step-two lattice is
carried by the single factor $\tan(\pi s/2)$.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
The reflection formulas
\[
 \Gamma\Bigl(\frac{1-s}{2}\Bigr)
 \Gamma\Bigl(\frac{1+s}{2}\Bigr)
 =\frac{\pi}{\cos(\pi s/2)},\qquad
 \Gamma\Bigl(\frac{s}{2}\Bigr)
 \Gamma\Bigl(1-\frac{s}{2}\Bigr)
 =\frac{\pi}{\sin(\pi s/2)},
\]
together with $\Gamma(1+s/2)=(s/2)\Gamma(s/2)$, give
\eqref{eq:rhatfactor}.  Formula \eqref{eq:rhatformal} is the standard
formal logarithmic expansion of the Gamma quotient at $z=s/2$,
\emph{squared} (whence the factor $2$ in the exponent), followed by
exponentiation; the leading term is $s\cdot(s/2)^{-1}=2$.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:gammaquadrature}
Define the formal forcing
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fgammahat}
 \widehat{\mathsf f}_{\Gamma}(s)
 :=-\frac{(2s-1)\,\widehat{\mathsf r}(s)}{4s^2(s-1)}
 \in s^{-2}\mathbb Q[[s^{-1}]],
\end{equation}
and let
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Qgammahat}
 \widehat Q_{\Gamma}
 :=\frac1{2\sinh\partial_s}\,\widehat{\mathsf f}_{\Gamma}
 \in s^{-1}\mathbb Q[[s^{-1}]].
\end{equation}
For a fixed step-two lattice avoiding the poles, the Gamma part of the
convergent quadrature has the exact factorisation
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Qgammafactor}
 \sum_{k\ge0}\mathsf f_{\Gamma}(s-1-2k)
 =-\cot\frac{\pi s}{2}
   \sum_{k\ge0}\widehat{\mathsf f}_{\Gamma}(s-1-2k).
\end{equation}
In the upper half-plane the second sum is asymptotic to
$\widehat Q_{\Gamma}(s)$ up to an exponentially small error
(Lemma~\ref{lem:vertical}(c)); this expansion holds in sectors off the
real axis, not on real step-two lattices.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:rhat},
$\mathsf f_{\Gamma}(\varsigma)=
\tan(\pi\varsigma/2)\,\widehat{\mathsf f}_{\Gamma}(\varsigma)$.
For $\varsigma=s-1-2k$,
\[
 \tan\frac{\pi(s-1-2k)}2=-\cot\frac{\pi s}2,
\]
independently of $k$, which proves \eqref{eq:Qgammafactor}.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:osc-remainder}
Let $Q=\mathsf K_2/\mathsf K_0$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Tdef}
 T(s)=\sum_{k\ge0}\widehat{\mathsf f}_{\Gamma}(s-1-2k).
\end{equation}
On a fixed step-two lattice the quadrature \eqref{eq:quadrature} reads
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Qdecomp}
 Q(s)=c_*(s_0)+Q_{\rm rat}(s)-\cot\frac{\pi s}{2}\,T(s),
\end{equation}
with $Q_{\rm rat}$ given by \eqref{eq:Qrat}, and the identity
\eqref{eq:onefun} is equivalent to
\begin{equation}\label{eq:osc-isolated}
 \operatorname{Im}\mathcal A
 =-\frac12\,T(s)+\tan\frac{\pi s}{2}\,\mathcal E(s),
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Edef}
 \mathcal E(s)=\frac{c_*(s_0)}2+\frac{Q_{\rm rat}(s)}2
 -\operatorname{Re}\mathcal A-\frac{\psi'(s)}4.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
Since
$\pi\mathsf K_0/\mathsf S_0=\tan(\pi s/2)$,
formula \eqref{eq:onefun} reads
\[
 \operatorname{Im}\mathcal A
 =\frac12\tan\frac{\pi s}{2}\,Q(s)
 -\tan\frac{\pi s}{2}
  \left(\operatorname{Re}\mathcal A+\frac{\psi'(s)}4\right).
\]
The decomposition \eqref{eq:Qdecomp} is \eqref{eq:quadrature} combined with
Corollary~\ref{cor:rational-quadrature} and \eqref{eq:Qgammafactor}.  Inserting
it, the product of tangent and cotangent is $1$, and
\eqref{eq:osc-isolated}--\eqref{eq:Edef} follow.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rem:Delta}
By Corollary~\ref{cor:R},
the series $\sum_n\operatorname{Re}g_nZ^{-n}$ is the asymptotic
expansion of
\[
 \int_0^\infty\frac{t\,e^{2st}}{\sinh2t}\,dt
 =\frac18\,\psi'\!\left(\frac{1-s}{2}\right),
 \qquad \operatorname{Re}s<0.
\]
On the real axis the function $\operatorname{Re}\mathcal A$ does not
coincide with this function: at $s=1$ the value
$\operatorname{Re}\mathcal A=-\pi^2/48$ is finite
(Theorem~\ref{thm:anchor1} below), whereas
$\psi'\bigl(\frac{1-s}2\bigr)$ has a double pole there.  We denote the
difference by
\[
 \Delta(s):=\operatorname{Re}\mathcal A(s)
 -\frac18\,\psi'\!\left(\frac{1-s}{2}\right).
\]
It is evaluated on the real axis in
Subsections~\ref{sec:boundarytransfer} and~\ref{sec:anchors} and, under
a periodicity hypothesis, in closed form in
Proposition~\ref{prop:realaxis}.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:GaussDerivativeFree}
Write $F^{\uparrow}(a,b)={}_2F_1^{\uparrow}(a,b;a+b;2)$.  Then
\begin{align}
 a\,{}_2F_1^{\uparrow}(a+1,b;a+b;2)+(b-a)\,F^{\uparrow}(a,b)
   +b\,{}_2F_1^{\uparrow}(a-1,b;a+b;2)&=0,
 \label{eq:GaussAcontig}
\end{align}
and symmetrically in $(a,b)$.  Consequently the argument derivative is
eliminated:
\begin{align}
 2\,\partial_z{}_2F_1^{\uparrow}(a,b;a+b;z)\big|_{z=2}
 &=-b\bigl(F^{\uparrow}(a,b)
   +{}_2F_1^{\uparrow}(a-1,b;a+b;2)\bigr)\label{eq:derelimA}\\
 &=-a\bigl(F^{\uparrow}(a,b)
   +{}_2F_1^{\uparrow}(a,b-1;a+b;2)\bigr).\notag
\end{align}
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
Gauss's contiguous relation
$a(z-1)F(a+1,b;c;z)+(2a-c-az+bz)F(a,b;c;z)+(c-a)F(a-1,b;c;z)=0$
\cite{VidunasContiguous} at $c=a+b$, $z=2$ gives
\eqref{eq:GaussAcontig}.  The derivative contiguities
$zF'=a(F(a+1,b;c;z)-F)=b(F(a,b+1;c;z)-F)$ are standard
\cite[Sec.~15.5]{DLMF}; substituting \eqref{eq:GaussAcontig} and its
$(a,b)$-exchange gives \eqref{eq:derelimA}.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:secondsym}
With $d=d_s(\eta)=s^2-\eta^2$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:second-symmetric-contiguity}
 d\,(\vartheta+2s)(\vartheta+2s+1)\,Y_{s+1}(\eta;z)
 =2s(2s+1)\bigl((\vartheta+s)^2-\eta^2\bigr)Y_s(\eta;z),
\end{equation}
an identity of power series at $z=0$, hence of upper boundary values.  At
$z=2$ it is functionally independent of \eqref{eq:sdifferentialcontig}:
after use of the two hypergeometric equations, the determinant of the
coefficients of $Y_{s+1}(\eta;2)$ and $\partial_zY_{s+1}(\eta;2)$ is $4d^2$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
The quotient of the $n$th Taylor coefficients of $Y_{s+1}$ and $Y_s$ is
\[
 \frac{(n+s)^2-\eta^2}{s^2-\eta^2}\cdot
 \frac{2s(2s+1)}{(n+2s)(n+2s+1)},
\]
which is \eqref{eq:second-symmetric-contiguity} coefficientwise, since
$\vartheta z^n=nz^n$.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{thm:boundarytransfer}
At the upper boundary value, the pair
\eqref{eq:sdifferentialcontig}--\eqref{eq:second-symmetric-contiguity}
reduces to the two boundary rows
\begin{gather}
 2\,\partial_zY_{s+1}(\eta;2)+(2s+1)Y_{s+1}(\eta;2)
 =\frac{2s(2s+1)}{d}\,\partial_zY_s(\eta;2),
 \label{eq:first-boundary-row}\\
 d\,\bigl\{4(s-1)\partial_zY_{s+1}(\eta;2)
 +2(s^2-s-1+\eta^2)Y_{s+1}(\eta;2)\bigr\}\notag\\
 \qquad=2s(2s+1)\bigl\{-2\partial_zY_s(\eta;2)-d\,Y_s(\eta;2)\bigr\},
 \label{eq:second-boundary-row}
\end{gather}
an invertible two-by-two system.  Eliminating $\partial_zY_{s+1}$ gives the
scalar transfer
\begin{equation}\label{eq:scalar-boundary-transfer}
 Y_{s+1}(\eta;2^+)
 =\frac{s(2s+1)}{d^2}
 \bigl[2s\,\partial_zY_s(\eta;2^+)+d\,Y_s(\eta;2^+)\bigr],
\end{equation}
and, twice differentiated in $\eta$ at zero,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:scalar-second-jet-transfer}
 Y_{s+1}^{[2]}=\frac{2s+1}{s^3}
 \bigl(2s\,\dot Y_s^{[2]}+s^2Y_s^{[2]}-2Y_s^{[0]}\bigr)
 +\frac{4(2s+1)}{s^5}\bigl(2s\,\dot Y_s^{[0]}+s^2Y_s^{[0]}\bigr).
\end{equation}
Equivalently, with $U_s(\eta)=\bigl(Y_s(\eta;2^+),\,\partial_zY_s(\eta;2^+)\bigr)^T$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Mmatrix}
 U_{s+1}(\eta)=M_s(\eta)\,U_s(\eta),\qquad
 M_s(\eta)=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 \dfrac{s(2s+1)}{d}&
 \dfrac{2s^2(2s+1)}{d^2}\\[3mm]
 -\dfrac{s(2s+1)^2}{2d}&
 \dfrac{s(2s+1)\{d-s(2s+1)\}}{d^2}
 \end{pmatrix},
\end{equation}
and, since $M_s$ is even in $\eta$, the second derivatives with
respect to $\eta$ satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:jetprop}
 U_{s+1}^{[2]}=M_s(0)\,U_s^{[2]}+M_s''(0)\,U_s(0),
 \qquad U_s^{[2]}=\partial_\eta^2U_s(\eta)\big|_{\eta=0}=(Y_s^{[2]},\dot Y_s^{[2]})^T.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
The hypergeometric equation for $Y_{s+1}$, respectively $Y_s$, evaluated at
$z=2$, converts the second-order operators in
\eqref{eq:second-symmetric-contiguity} into the displayed first-order
boundary rows; \eqref{eq:first-boundary-row} is
\eqref{eq:sdifferentialcontig} at $z=2$.  The determinant of the system is
proportional to $d^2\ne0$; elimination gives
\eqref{eq:scalar-boundary-transfer}, and the first row returns
$\partial_zY_{s+1}$, i.e.\ \eqref{eq:Mmatrix}.  Formula
\eqref{eq:scalar-second-jet-transfer} is
$\partial_\eta^2$ of \eqref{eq:scalar-boundary-transfer} at $\eta=0$ using
$d=s^2-\eta^2$ and evenness in $\eta$; \eqref{eq:jetprop} is the same statement
for the pair.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:ps}
For the upper boundary value,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ps-explicit}
 \mathfrak p_s=-\frac s2+
 \frac{i\,s^2(s+\frac12)}{2(2s+1)}
 \left[\frac{\Gamma(\frac{s+1}{2})}
 {\Gamma(\frac{s+2}{2})}\right]^2.
\end{equation}
Consequently the coefficients in \eqref{eq:jetprop} are all explicit, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:J-exact-adjacent}
 J_s=\frac1s+
 \frac{2s\mathfrak p_s+s^2}{2s}
 \left(R_{s+1}-R_s-\frac4{s^2}\right):
\end{equation}
thus $J_s$ is expressed through the first difference $R_{s+1}-R_s$.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
At $\eta=0$, \eqref{eq:scalar-boundary-transfer} reads
$Y_{s+1}^{[0]}=\frac{2s+1}{s^3}(2s\,\dot Y_s^{[0]}+s^2Y_s^{[0]})$, so
$\mathfrak p_s=\frac{s^2}{2(2s+1)}\frac{Y_{s+1}^{[0]}}{Y_s^{[0]}}-\frac s2$.  By
Lemma~\ref{lem:quadeval},
$Y_{s+1}^{[0]}/Y_s^{[0]}=e^{i\pi/2}\,(s+\tfrac12)\,
[\Gamma(\frac{s+1}2)/\Gamma(\frac{s+2}2)]^2$, which gives
\eqref{eq:ps-explicit}.  Formula \eqref{eq:J-exact-adjacent} follows by
taking two $\eta$-derivatives at $\eta=0$ of the logarithm of
\[
 \frac{Y_{s+1}(\eta;2^+)}{Y_s(\eta;2^+)}
 =\frac{s(2s+1)}{d^2}\,\Bigl\{2s\,\frac{\partial_zY_s(\eta;2^+)}{Y_s(\eta;2^+)}+d\Bigr\}.
\]
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:nopolyinv}
The transfer \eqref{eq:Mmatrix} is invertible away from $s^2=\eta^2$, and
it is two-dimensional: formula \eqref{eq:J-exact-adjacent} exchanges the
derivative $J_s$ for the adjacent value $R_{s+1}$ but does not eliminate
it.  The recurrence therefore determines $(R_s,J_s)$ on a class
$s_*+\mathbb Z$ once the pair $(R_{s_*},J_{s_*})$ is known at one point
of the class.  Terminating points $s=-N$ cannot be used for this
purpose, because $2s=-2N$ is then a pole of the denominator parameter
away from $\eta=0$.  The next subsection supplies these initial values,
which we call \emph{anchors}.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
\label{thm:anchor1}
At $s=1$, $Y_1(0;z)={}_2F_1(1,1;2;z)=-\log(1-z)/z$, so for the upper
boundary convention
\begin{equation}\label{eq:y1}
 Y_1^{[0]}=\frac{i\pi}{2},\qquad
 \dot Y_1^{[0]}=-\frac12-\frac{i\pi}{4}.
\end{equation}
Furthermore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:R1J1}
 R_1=-\frac{\pi^2}{6}-\frac{7i}{\pi}\,\zeta(3),
 \qquad
 J_1=2\log2-\frac{7}{\pi^2}\,\zeta(3)-\frac{i\pi}{3},
\end{equation}
equivalently
\[
 Y_1^{[2]}=\frac72\zeta(3)-\frac{i\pi^3}{12},
 \qquad
 \dot Y_1^{[2]}
 =\frac{\pi^2}{4}-\frac74\zeta(3)
 +i\Bigl(\pi\log2+\frac{\pi^3}{24}\Bigr).
\]
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
Formulae \eqref{eq:y1} are immediate from $\log(1-z)\to-i\pi$.  Define
$I(u)=\int_0^u\log^2(1-t)\,t^{-1}\,dt$; an antiderivative calculation
gives
\[
 I(u)=\log^2(1-u)\log u
 +2\log(1-u)\operatorname{Li}_2(1-u)-2\operatorname{Li}_3(1-u)+2\zeta(3),
\]
whence, at the upper boundary,
$I(2^+)=\frac72\zeta(3)-\pi^2\log2+\frac{i\pi^3}{6}$.  The transverse
variational equation at $s=1$ and reduction of order over the explicit
solution $Y_1(0;z)$ yield
\[
 R_1=-2\int_0^{2^+}
 \frac{I(u)}{(1-u)\log^2(1-u)}\,du,
 \qquad
 J_1=-\frac{2}{\pi^2}\,I(2^+),
\]
which proves the $J_1$ formula.  For $R_1$, substitute $x=\log(1-u)$;
since $dI/dx=-x^2e^x/(1-e^x)$, integration by parts gives
\[
 R_1=2\left[-\frac{I}{x}
 +x\log(1-e^x)+\operatorname{Li}_2(e^x)\right]_{x=0}^{x=-i\pi},
\]
and the endpoint values $\operatorname{Li}_2(1)=\pi^2/6$,
$\operatorname{Li}_2(-1)=-\pi^2/12$,
$\operatorname{Li}_3(-1)=-\frac34\zeta(3)$ with
$\log(-1-i0)=-i\pi$ give \eqref{eq:R1J1}; the $\log2$ terms cancel
exactly.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
\label{thm:euleranchor}
Let $0<\operatorname{Re}s_*<1$ with $Y_{s_*}^{[0]}\ne0$.  For
$\varepsilon>0$ put
\begin{gather*}
 \mathsf w_{s_*,\varepsilon}(t)=t^{s_*-1}(1-t)^{s_*-1}
 \bigl(1-(2+i\varepsilon)t\bigr)^{-s_*},\qquad
 \mathsf T_\varepsilon(t)=\frac{t}{1-(2+i\varepsilon)t},\\
 \mathsf L_\varepsilon(t)=\log t-\log(1-t)+\log\bigl(1-(2+i\varepsilon)t\bigr),
\end{gather*}
and the normalised complex expectation
$\langle f\rangle_{s_*,\varepsilon}=
\int_0^1\mathsf w_{s_*,\varepsilon}f\,dt\big/
\int_0^1\mathsf w_{s_*,\varepsilon}\,dt$; all integrals converge absolutely
for every $\varepsilon>0$.  Write
$\langle f\rangle_{s_*}=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}
\langle f\rangle_{s_*,\varepsilon}$ whenever the limit exists.  Then
$\langle\mathsf L^2\rangle_{s_*}$ exists as an absolutely convergent integral
at $\varepsilon=0$ (boundary values $1-2t-i0$), the $\mathsf T$-moments exist
as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ limits (equivalently, as absolutely
convergent integrals over any contour from $0$ to $1$ that leaves the
segment near $t=\frac12$ into the upper half-plane), and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:euleranchor}
 R_{s_*}=-2\psi'(s_*)+\langle\mathsf L^2\rangle_{s_*},
 \qquad
 J_{s_*}=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\Bigl[
 s_*\bigl\{\langle \mathsf L_\varepsilon^2\mathsf T_\varepsilon
 \rangle_{s_*,\varepsilon}
 -\langle \mathsf L_\varepsilon^2\rangle_{s_*,\varepsilon}
 \langle \mathsf T_\varepsilon\rangle_{s_*,\varepsilon}\bigr\}
 -2\langle \mathsf L_\varepsilon \mathsf T_\varepsilon\rangle_{s_*,\varepsilon}
 \Bigr].
\end{equation}
Consequently every \emph{real} residual class $s_0+\mathbb Z$ avoiding
the parameter poles and the zeros of the boundary solution carries a
canonical anchor: choose the representative $s_*\in s_0+\mathbb Z$
with $0<s_*<1$, the integer class being covered by
Theorem~\ref{thm:anchor1} at $s_*=1$; the invertible transfer
\eqref{eq:Mmatrix}--\eqref{eq:jetprop} and its inverse then determine
$(R_s,J_s)$ uniquely on the whole class, independently of the
representative used.
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
\emph{Convergence and existence of the limits.}  For $\varepsilon>0$
the factor $1-(2+i\varepsilon)t$ is bounded away from zero on $[0,1]$,
so all moments converge absolutely; at $\varepsilon=0$ the integrand of
$\langle\mathsf L^2\rangle_{s_*}$ is
$O\bigl(|1-2t|^{-\operatorname{Re}s_*}\log^2|1-2t|\bigr)$ near
$t=\frac12$, absolutely integrable for
$\operatorname{Re}s_*<1$, while the $\mathsf T$-moments carry an extra
factor $(1-2t-i0)^{-1}$ and are \emph{not} absolutely convergent at
$\varepsilon=0$: they must be taken as the stated limits.  The limits
exist by contour deformation: the singularity of the integrand sits at
$t_\varepsilon=1/(2+i\varepsilon)$, which lies \emph{below} the real
segment and tends to $\frac12$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$; the
integrand is analytic in $t$ in the upper half-disc around
$t=\frac12$, so $\int_0^1$ may be replaced, for every
$\varepsilon\ge0$, by the integral over the contour
$\mathcal C_{r_0}$ which follows the segment but crosses a semicircle of
fixed radius $r_0\in(0,\tfrac14)$ \emph{above} $t=\frac12$.  On
$\mathcal C_{r_0}$ the integrands converge uniformly as
$\varepsilon\downarrow0$ (the denominator is bounded away from zero),
so each moment tends to the corresponding absolutely convergent
$\mathcal C_{r_0}$-integral, which is independent of $r_0$; this
realises the boundary prescription $1-2t-i0$.

\emph{The formulae.}  Euler's integral representation gives, for $\eta$
near zero and $\varepsilon\ge0$ interpreted as above,
\[
 Y_{s_*}(\eta;2^+)=
 \frac{\Gamma(2s_*)}
 {\Gamma(s_*+\eta)\Gamma(s_*-\eta)}
 \int_{\mathcal C_{r_0}}\mathsf w_{s_*}(t)\,e^{\eta \mathsf L(t)}\,dt.
\]
The family is even in $\eta$, hence $\langle\mathsf L\rangle_{s_*}=0$.  Two
$\eta$-derivatives of the logarithm give the $R_{s_*}$ formula, the
$-2\psi'(s_*)$ coming from the Gamma prefactor.  For fixed $\eta$,
logarithmic $z$-differentiation of the integral has score $s_*\mathsf T$ at
$\eta=0$, while $\partial_z\mathsf L=-\mathsf T$; differentiating the normalised second
moment gives the $J_{s_*}$ formula, first at $\varepsilon>0$ and then
in the limit, which is \eqref{eq:euleranchor}.  The transfer matrix is
invertible away from its explicit divisors, so the anchor propagates
uniquely in both directions; if two admissible representatives are
chosen, Euler's formula identifies both with the same analytic boundary
solution, and uniqueness of the propagation proves independence of the
choice.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- theorem-16: body_md -->
\label{thm:realkernel}
As formal series in $Z^{-1}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:realkernel}
 \sum_{n\ge1}\operatorname{Re}g_n\,Z^{-n}
 =\frac1{16}\,\psi'\!\Bigl(\frac{Z+1}4\Bigr)
 -\frac1{16}\,\psi'\!\Bigl(\frac{Z+3}4\Bigr)
 +\frac14\,\psi'\!\Bigl(\frac{Z+1}2\Bigr),
\end{equation}
where each $\psi'$ stands for its Bernoulli asymptotic expansion.
<!-- end theorem-16 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
From $\psi'(x)=\int_0^\infty ue^{-xu}(1-e^{-u})^{-1}\,du$ with $u=4t$,
$4t$, $2t$ respectively, the right side of \eqref{eq:realkernel} is the
Watson expansion of $\int_0^\infty te^{-Zt}\varphi_{\mathrm R}(t)\,dt$ with
\[
 \varphi_{\mathrm R}(t)=\frac{e^{-t}-e^{-3t}}{1-e^{-4t}}+\frac{e^{-t}}{1-e^{-2t}}
 =\frac1{2\cosh t}+\frac1{2\sinh t}.
\]
Watson's correspondence $\int_0^\infty t^ne^{-Zt}dt=n!\,Z^{-n-1}$ is
coefficientwise exact, so the $n$-th coefficient of the right side of
\eqref{eq:realkernel} is the $(n-1)$-st Taylor coefficient of
$t\varphi_{\mathrm R}(t)$.  By Corollary~\ref{cor:R},
$\sum_{n\ge1}\operatorname{Re}g_n\,t^{n-1}/(n-1)!
=\operatorname{Re}\Phi(t)/t=te^t/\sinh2t
=t(\operatorname{sech}t+\operatorname{csch}t)/2=t\varphi_{\mathrm R}(t)$,
which proves \eqref{eq:realkernel}.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lem:vertical}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\upshape(a)] Fix $0<\theta_0<1$.  For every $N$ there is $C_N$ such
that, uniformly on the bilateral cone
$|\operatorname{Re}Z|\le\theta_0\,|\operatorname{Im}Z|$,
$|\operatorname{Im}Z|\ge y_{\min}(\theta_0,N)$ (\emph{both} signs of
$\operatorname{Im}Z$, in particular on every vertical strip)
\[
 \Bigl|\mathcal A-\sum_{n=1}^Ng_nZ^{-n}\Bigr|\le C_N\,|Z|^{-N-1}.
\]
\item[\upshape(b)] On every closed subsector of
$|\arg(\pm is)|<\pi/2$ the closed blocks $\mathsf K_0$,
$\mathsf S_0$, $\widehat{\mathsf r}$, $Q_{\rm rat}$ and the trigamma
functions are asymptotic to their Bernoulli--Stirling series, with
uniform remainders after each truncation.
\item[\upshape(c)] For every $\delta>0$ and every $N$, uniformly on
$\operatorname{Im}s\ge\delta|s|$,
\[
 \Bigl|T(s)-\sum_{j=1}^N\omega_j\,s^{-j}\Bigr|
 \le C_{\delta,N}\,|s|^{-N-1}
 +C_\delta\,\frac{e^{-\pi\operatorname{Im}s}}{\operatorname{Im}s},
 \qquad
 T(s)=\sum_{k\ge0}\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma(s-1-2k),
\]
where $\sum_j\omega_js^{-j}$ is the formal series
$\widehat Q_\Gamma=(2\sinh\partial_s)^{-1}\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma$ of
Proposition~\ref{prop:formal-sinh}.
\end{enumerate}
The mirror statements hold in the lower half-plane by Schwarz
reflection, with the same (rational) coefficients.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
Appendix~\ref{app:vertical}: (a) is
Proposition~\ref{prop:bilateral}, proved from the coefficient bound
$|G_n|\le C(n+1)!\,2^{-n/2}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:hankel}), the elementary
product inequality $(j+1)\le\sqrt2\,|Z-j|$ valid on the cone
(Lemma~\ref{lem:tailsum}), and the exact function-level identity
\eqref{eq:midpoint2F1} between the convergent inverse-factorial series
\eqref{eq:F} and the boundary family $\mathcal H$; (b) is
Lemma~\ref{lem:blocksasy}; (c) is
Proposition~\ref{prop:latticetail}, proved from a two-regime uniform
expansion of $\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma$ on horizontal lines
(Stirling on $|\arg\varsigma|\le\tfrac34\pi$; reflection, a Beta-integral
bound and $\cot(\pi\varsigma/2)=-i+O(e^{-\pi\operatorname{Im}\varsigma})$ on
the left regime), the $k\le|s|$ / $k>|s|$ splitting of the lattice
sum, the uniform Hurwitz--Bernoulli expansions of the moment sums
$\sum_k(s-1-2k)^{-j}$, and the formal uniqueness of
Proposition~\ref{prop:formal-sinh}.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:realaxis}
Define the analytic extension of the difference $\Delta$ of
Remark~\ref{rem:Delta},
\[
 \widetilde\Delta(s):=\frac{\mathcal A^{\uparrow}(s)+\mathcal A^{\downarrow}(s)}2
 -\frac1{16}\,\psi'\!\Bigl(\frac{1-s}2\Bigr)
 +\frac1{16}\,\psi'\!\Bigl(1-\frac s2\Bigr)
 -\frac14\,\psi'(1-s),
\]
with $\mathcal A^{\uparrow\!,\downarrow}$ the two boundary components
of Appendix~\ref{app:sub-relation}, so that
$\widetilde\Delta=\operatorname{Re}\mathcal A-{}$(trigamma part) on the real axis.
Assume
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\upshape(P)] $\widetilde\Delta$ is $2$-periodic, with poles confined to the
odd class, of order at most two.
\end{enumerate}
Then, on the real axis,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ReND-closed}
 \operatorname{Re}\mathcal A(s)
 =\frac1{16}\,\psi'\!\Bigl(\frac{1-s}2\Bigr)
 -\frac1{16}\,\psi'\!\Bigl(1-\frac s2\Bigr)
 +\frac14\,\psi'(1-s)
 -\frac{\pi^2}8\,\sec^2\frac{\pi s}2 ,
\end{equation}
with convergent trigamma functions; that is,
$\widetilde\Delta=-\frac{\pi^2}8\sec^2\frac{\pi s}2$.  Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Eclosed}
 \mathcal E(s)=\frac{\pi^2}8\,\sec^2\frac{\pi s}2
 -\frac{\pi^2}4\,\csc^2(\pi s),
\end{equation}
and the identity \eqref{eq:osc-isolated} becomes explicit:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Imclosed-fn}
 \operatorname{Im}\mathcal A(s)
 =-\frac12\,T(s)+\tan\frac{\pi s}2\,\mathcal E(s),
 \qquad T(s)=\sum_{k\ge0}\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma(s-1-2k).
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
The function $\widetilde\Delta$ decays at both vertical ends of the strip
$\operatorname{Re}s\in[0,2]$: by the two-component
relation \eqref{eq:tworelation-X} and Lemma~\ref{lem:vertical}(a), in
the upper half-plane
$\mathcal A^{\downarrow}=-\tfrac i2X+O(e^{-\pi\operatorname{Im}s})$
while $\mathcal A^{\uparrow}$ is asymptotic to the series $\sum_ng_nZ^{-n}$, so
$(\mathcal A^{\uparrow}+\mathcal A^{\downarrow})/2$ is asymptotic to
the \emph{real} trigamma series of Theorem~\ref{thm:realkernel}, which
the convergent trigamma part reproduces (Lemma~\ref{lem:vertical}(b));
the lower end is the mirror statement.  Under hypothesis (P) the
classification lemma (Lemma~\ref{lem:cylclass}, with $k_1=2$, $k_0=0$)
gives $\widetilde\Delta=c\,\sec^2\frac{\pi s}2$ for some constant $c$.  The
principal part at $s=1$ determines $c$: the trigamma part of $\widetilde\Delta$ has the
double pole
$-\bigl[\tfrac1{16}\cdot4+\tfrac14\bigr](s-1)^{-2}=-\tfrac12(s-1)^{-2}$,
while $\mathcal A^{\uparrow\!,\downarrow}$ are finite at $s=1$
(Theorem~\ref{thm:anchor1}), and
$\sec^2\frac{\pi s}2\sim4/(\pi^2(s-1)^2)$; hence $c=-\pi^2/8$.  The
finite part at $s=1$ is consistent with the value given by the
polylogarithmic evaluation:
$\operatorname{Re}R_1/8=-\pi^2/48$
(Theorem~\ref{thm:anchor1}).  Formula \eqref{eq:Eclosed} follows from
\eqref{eq:Edef} with $c_*(s_0)=0$
(Theorem~\ref{thm:czero}) and the reflection
$\psi'(s)=\pi^2\csc^2(\pi s)-\psi'(1-s)$; and \eqref{eq:Imclosed-fn} is
\eqref{eq:osc-isolated}.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
We describe the structure of the argument; the details are given in
Appendix~\ref{app:sub-imclosed}.  The two boundary components obey the exact
two-component relation (Lemma~\ref{lem:tworelation},
Corollary~\ref{cor:Edef-czero})
\[
 \Bigl(\tan\frac{\pi s}2-i\Bigr)\mathcal A^{\uparrow}
 +\Bigl(\tan\frac{\pi s}2+i\Bigr)\mathcal A^{\downarrow}
 =-\,T(s)+\tan\frac{\pi s}2
 \Bigl(Q_{\rm rat}(s)-\frac{\psi'(s)}2\Bigr)=:X(s),
\]
which uses the vanishing of the lattice constant
(Theorem~\ref{thm:czero}).  Along the vertical line
$s=-\tfrac12+iY$, $Y\to-\infty$, one has
$\tan\frac{\pi s}2+i=O(e^{-\pi|Y|})$, so that the term in
$\mathcal A^{\downarrow}$ is exponentially small, $\tan\frac{\pi s}2-i\to-2i$, and
$\mathcal A^{\uparrow}$ is asymptotic to $\sum_ng_nZ^{-n}$ by the
\emph{bilateral} expansion of Lemma~\ref{lem:vertical}(a); hence
$\mathcal A^{\uparrow}=\tfrac i2X+O(e^{-\pi|Y|})$.  Expanding $X$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:vertical}(b),(c), with
$\tan\frac{\pi s}2=-i+O(e^{-\pi|Y|})$, and using the formal
reflection parity $S_\psi(1-s)=-S_\psi(s)$ of the Stirling series of
$\psi'$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:stirparity}) to put the real part into
trigamma-kernel form, one obtains exactly
\eqref{eq:formal-tangent}: the real part is
Theorem~\ref{thm:realkernel}, and the imaginary part is
\eqref{eq:Imgclosed}.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lem:kernelW}
Write the series \eqref{eq:fgammahat} in powers of $Z^{-1}$,
$\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma=\sum_{n\ge2}f_nZ^{-n}$, and let
$\varphi(t)=\sum_{n\ge2}f_nt^{n-1}/(n-1)!$ be its Borel transform.  Then
the Borel transform of $\widehat Q_\Gamma$ is $\varphi(t)/(2\sinh2t)$,
and
\[
 W(t)=-\frac{\varphi(t)}{4t}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
Since $s\pm1$ corresponds to $Z\mp2$, the equation
$\widehat Q_\Gamma(s+1)-\widehat Q_\Gamma(s-1)=\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma(s)$
reads $\widehat Q_\Gamma(Z-2)-\widehat Q_\Gamma(Z+2)=\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma(Z)$.
A shift $Z\mapsto Z+c$ multiplies Borel transforms by $e^{-ct}$
(Remark~\ref{rem:borel}), so the Borel transform $\widehat q(t)$ of
$\widehat Q_\Gamma$ satisfies
$(e^{2t}-e^{-2t})\,\widehat q(t)=\varphi(t)$.  By
\eqref{eq:Imgclosed},
$\operatorname{Im}\Phi(t)/t=-\tfrac12\widehat q(t)=-\varphi(t)/(4\sinh2t)$,
and the formula for $W$ follows from \eqref{eq:Wdef}.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lem:genocchi}
The formal exponent of Lemma~\ref{lem:rhat}, written in the variable
$Z$, is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:BZ}
 \log\frac{\widehat{\mathsf r}}2=\mathsf b(Z)
 =\sum_{j\ge1}b_j\,(Z-1)^{1-2j},
 \qquad
 b_j=\frac{2^{2j-1}\mathfrak G_{2j}}{(2j)(2j-1)},
\end{equation}
and coefficientwise $\mathsf b$ is the Watson expansion of
$-\int_0^\infty e^{-(Z-1)t}\,t^{-1}\tanh t\,dt$.  Moreover
\begin{equation}\label{eq:nubj}
 \nu_2(b_j)=2j-2-\nu_2(j)\ \ge\ 0,
\end{equation}
with equality only for $j=1$, where $b_1=\mathfrak G_2=-1$.
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
In \eqref{eq:rhatformal} the bracket is
$\mathcal B_{n+1}(0)-\mathcal B_{n+1}(\tfrac12)=(2-2^{-n})\mathcal B_{n+1}$ by
$\mathcal B_m(\tfrac12)=(2^{1-m}-1)\mathcal B_m$; it vanishes for even $n\ge2$ (odd-index
Bernoulli numbers vanish), and for $n=2j-1$ the coefficient of
$s^{1-2j}$ is
$(2^{2j+1}-2)\mathcal B_{2j}/((2j)(2j-1))=-\mathfrak G_{2j}/((2j)(2j-1))$.
Substituting $s^{-1}=-2/(Z-1)$ gives \eqref{eq:BZ}.  For the kernel form,
$\tanh t=\sum_{j\ge1}2^{2j}(2^{2j}-1)\mathcal B_{2j}\,t^{2j-1}/(2j)!$, so
$-(2j-2)!\,[t^{2j-1}]\tanh t
=2^{2j-1}\mathfrak G_{2j}/((2j)(2j-1))=b_j$, and Watson's correspondence
$(Z-1)^{1-2j}\leftrightarrow t^{2j-2}/(2j-2)!$ is coefficientwise exact.
For \eqref{eq:nubj}: by von Staudt--Clausen $\nu_2(\mathcal B_{2j})=-1$, hence
$\mathfrak G_{2j}=2(1-2^{2j})\mathcal B_{2j}$ is an odd integer, and
$\nu_2(b_j)=(2j-1)-\nu_2\bigl((2j)(2j-1)\bigr)=2j-2-\nu_2(j)$; finally
$\nu_2(j)\le\log_2j\le2j-2$, with equality throughout only at $j=1$.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{lem:parityF}
As formal series in $Z^{-1}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Bparity}
 \mathsf b(Z)+\sum_{j\ge1}b_j(Z+1)^{1-2j}
 =\log\frac{Z-1}{Z+1},
\end{equation}
and consequently the forcing of \eqref{eq:fgammahat}, written in
$Z^{-1}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:FZform}
 \widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma
 =\mathsf F(Z):=-\,\frac{4Z\,e^{\mathsf b(Z)}}{(Z-1)^2(Z+1)},
\end{equation}
is an \emph{even} series: $[Z^{-n}]\mathsf F=0$ for odd $n$.
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:genocchi} the left side of \eqref{eq:Bparity} is the
Watson expansion of
\[
 -\int_0^\infty e^{-Zt}\,(e^{t}+e^{-t})\,\frac{\tanh t}t\,dt
 =-\int_0^\infty e^{-Zt}\,\frac{2\sinh t}t\,dt,
\]
whose coefficient series is
$-2\sum_{k\ge0}Z^{-2k-1}/(2k+1)=\log\frac{Z-1}{Z+1}$.  Formula
\eqref{eq:FZform} is the substitution $s=(1-Z)/2$ in
\eqref{eq:fgammahat}: $2s-1=-Z$, $4s^2(s-1)=-(Z-1)^2(Z+1)/2$, and
$\widehat{\mathsf r}=2e^{\mathsf b}$.  Then
\[
 \frac{\mathsf F(-Z)}{\mathsf F(Z)}
 =e^{-\bigl(\mathsf b(Z)+\sum_jb_j(Z+1)^{1-2j}\bigr)}\cdot\frac{Z-1}{Z+1}=1
\]
by \eqref{eq:Bparity}, which is evenness.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{lem:dominance}
Write $e^{\mathsf b(Z)}=\sum_{N\ge0}u_N(Z-1)^{-N}$.  Then for every $N\ge0$,
\[
 \nu_2(u_N)=-\nu_2(N!),
\]
and $N!\,u_N$ is a $2$-adic unit.
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
Expanding the exponential,
$u_N=\sum_\lambda\prod_j b_j^{m_j}/m_j!$, the sum over partitions
$\lambda$ of $N$ into odd parts $2j-1$ with multiplicities $m_j$.  For
any $\lambda$, since every $\nu_2(b_j)\ge0$ and
$\prod_jm_j!\mid\ell!$ with $\ell=\sum_jm_j\le N$ (multinomial
integrality),
\[
 \nu_2\Bigl(\prod_jb_j^{m_j}\big/\!\prod_jm_j!\Bigr)
 \ \ge\ -\nu_2\Bigl(\prod_jm_j!\Bigr)\ \ge\ -\nu_2(\ell!)\ \ge\
 -\nu_2(N!).
\]
The all-ones partition contributes $b_1^N/N!=(-1)^N/N!$, of valuation
exactly $-\nu_2(N!)$.  Every other partition has some part
$2j-1\ge3$, hence $\sum_jm_j\nu_2(b_j)\ge\nu_2(b_j)\ge1$ by
\eqref{eq:nubj}, so its valuation is at least $1-\nu_2(N!)$: strictly
larger.  By the ultrametric inequality the valuation of $u_N$ is exactly
$-\nu_2(N!)$ and $N!\,u_N\equiv(-1)^N\pmod2$.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- theorem-17: body_md -->
\label{thm:arithlaw}
For every $m\ge0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:arithlaw}
 \nu_2\bigl([Z^{-(2m+2)}]\,\mathsf F\bigr)=2-2m+s_2(m).
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-17 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
Expand the rational prefactor of \eqref{eq:FZform} in $Z^{-1}$:
\[
 \frac{-4Z}{(Z-1)^2(Z+1)}=-4\sum_{k\ge0}c_k\,Z^{-k-2},
 \qquad
 c_k=[x^k]\,\frac1{(1-x)^2(1+x)}=\Bigl\lfloor\frac k2\Bigr\rfloor+1
 \in\mathbb Z,
\]
and
$(Z-1)^{-N}=\sum_{m\ge N}\binom{m-1}{N-1}Z^{-m}$ for $N\ge1$, with integer
coefficients.  Hence, for $n\ge2$,
\[
 [Z^{-n}]\mathsf F
 =-4\sum_{N=0}^{n-2}u_N\,M_{n,N},
 \qquad
 M_{n,N}=\sum_{m=N}^{n-2}c_{\,n-2-m}\binom{m-1}{N-1}
 \in\mathbb Z\quad(N\ge1),
\]
with $M_{n,0}=c_{n-2}$; in particular $M_{n,n-2}=1$.  The term $N=n-2$ contributes
$-4u_{n-2}$, of valuation exactly $2-\nu_2((n-2)!)$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:dominance}.  For $N\le n-3$ and $n$ \emph{even},
\[
 \nu_2(u_NM_{n,N})\ \ge\ -\nu_2(N!)\ \ge\ -\nu_2((n-3)!)
 =-\nu_2((n-2)!)+\nu_2(n-2)\ \ge\ -\nu_2((n-2)!)+1 ,
\]
so every other term has strictly larger valuation.  Hence
$\nu_2([Z^{-n}]\mathsf F)=2-\nu_2((n-2)!)$ exactly; with $n=2m+2$ this
is $2-(2m-s_2(2m))=2-2m+s_2(m)$.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- theorem-18: body_md -->
\label{thm:dyadicW}
For every $m\ge0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:wm-kernel}
