 w_m=-\,\frac{[Z^{-(2m+2)}]\,\mathsf F}{4\,(2m+1)!}\,,
\end{equation}
and consequently
$\nu_2(w_m)=-2\,\nu_2\bigl((2m)!\bigr)$.
<!-- end theorem-18 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:kernelW}, $W(t)=-\varphi(t)/(4t)$ with
$\varphi(t)=\sum_nf_nt^{n-1}/(n-1)!$ the Borel transform of
$\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma=\mathsf F$; the coefficient of $t^{2m}$ in
$W$ is therefore $-f_{2m+2}/(4(2m+1)!)$, which is
\eqref{eq:wm-kernel}.  Then Theorem~\ref{thm:arithlaw} and
$\nu_2((2m+1)!)=\nu_2((2m)!)=2m-s_2(m)$ give
$\nu_2(w_m)=\bigl(2-2m+s_2(m)\bigr)-2-\bigl(2m-s_2(m)\bigr)
=-2\bigl(2m-s_2(m)\bigr)=-2\nu_2((2m)!)$.
<!-- end proof-53 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{lem:weights2}
Put
\[
 \mathsf d(t)=\frac{2t}{\sinh2t}=\sum_{k\ge0}\mathsf d_kt^{2k},\qquad
 \mathsf e(t)=\frac{\sinh2t}{2t}=\sum_{k\ge0}\mathsf e_kt^{2k},
\]
so that $\mathsf d(t)\,\mathsf e(t)=1$.  Then
$\mathsf d_0=\mathsf e_0=1$ and
$\nu_2(\mathsf d_k)=\nu_2(\mathsf e_k)=s_2(k)$ for every $k\ge1$.
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
$\mathsf e_k=2^{2k}/(2k+1)!$ gives
$\nu_2(\mathsf e_k)=2k-\bigl(2k+1-s_2(2k+1)\bigr)=s_2(k)$, using
$s_2(2k+1)=s_2(k)+1$.  For $\mathsf d$, the expansion
$x/\sinh x=\sum_k(2-2^{2k})\mathcal B_{2k}x^{2k}/(2k)!$ at $x=2t$ gives
$\mathsf d_k=(2-2^{2k})\mathcal B_{2k}\,2^{2k}/(2k)!$; for $k\ge1$,
$\nu_2(2-2^{2k})=1$ and $\nu_2(\mathcal B_{2k})=-1$ by von Staudt--Clausen, so
$\nu_2(\mathsf d_k)=1-1+2k-(2k-s_2(k))=s_2(k)$.
<!-- end proof-54 -->
<!-- theorem-19: body_md -->
\label{thm:tangentlaw}
For every $k\ge1$, $\operatorname{Im}g_{2k}=0$; and for every
$r\ge1$,
\[
 \nu_2\bigl(\operatorname{Im}g_{2r-1}\bigr)=-H_r,
 \qquad H_r=r+\nu_2\bigl((r-1)!\bigr).
\]
<!-- end theorem-19 -->
<!-- proof-55: body_md -->
\emph{Even indices.}  By Lemma~\ref{lem:parityF} the coefficients of
the odd powers of $Z^{-1}$ in $\mathsf F$ vanish, so its Borel
transform $\varphi$ is an odd function of $t$.  By
Lemma~\ref{lem:kernelW} the Borel transform of $\widehat Q_\Gamma$ is
$\varphi(t)/(2\sinh2t)$, an even function, so $\widehat q_n=0$ for even
$n$, and $\operatorname{Im}g_{2k}=-\widehat q_{2k}/2=0$ by
\eqref{eq:Imgclosed}.

\emph{Odd indices.}  Put
$\iota_m=[t^{2m}]\bigl(2\operatorname{Im}\Phi(t)/t\bigr)
=2\operatorname{Im}g_{2m+1}/(2m)!$ and
$\tau(m)=-2\nu_2((2m)!)=-4m+2s_2(m)$.  By the first part,
$2\operatorname{Im}\Phi(t)/t$ is an even series, and by
\eqref{eq:Wdef}
\[
 W(t)=\frac{2\operatorname{Im}\Phi(t)}t\;\mathsf e(t),
 \qquad
 \frac{2\operatorname{Im}\Phi(t)}t=W(t)\,\mathsf d(t),
\]
that is, $w_m=\sum_{k=0}^m\mathsf e_k\,\iota_{m-k}$ and
$\iota_m=\sum_{k=0}^m\mathsf d_k\,w_{m-k}$.  For $1\le k\le m$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:weights2} and the subadditivity
$s_2(m)\le s_2(m-k)+s_2(k)$ give
\[
 \bigl[s_2(k)+\tau(m-k)\bigr]-\tau(m)
 =s_2(k)+4k+2s_2(m-k)-2s_2(m)\ \ge\ 4k-s_2(k)\ >\ 0 .
\]
Since $\nu_2(w_j)=\tau(j)$ for every $j$ by
Theorem~\ref{thm:dyadicW}, every term with $k\ge1$ in
$\iota_m=\sum_k\mathsf d_kw_{m-k}$ has valuation strictly larger than
$\tau(m)$, while the term $k=0$ is $w_m$.  Hence
$\nu_2(\iota_m)=\tau(m)$, that is,
\[
 \nu_2\bigl(\operatorname{Im}g_{2m+1}\bigr)
 =\tau(m)-1+\nu_2\bigl((2m)!\bigr)
 =-\nu_2\bigl((2m)!\bigr)-1
 =-\bigl(2m+1-s_2(m)\bigr)=-H_{m+1}.
\]
<!-- end proof-55 -->
<!-- proof-56: body_md -->
The statements on $\operatorname{Im}g_{2k}$ and on
$\operatorname{Im}g_{2r-1}$ are Theorem~\ref{thm:tangentlaw}, and the
statement on $w_m$ is Theorem~\ref{thm:dyadicW}.  By \eqref{eq:A1B0},
\[
 \nu_2\bigl([A^1B^0]\kappa_r\bigr)=-(2r-1)-H_r=-E_r .
\]
<!-- end proof-56 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:dictionary}
For every $r\le8$, the polynomial $\kappa_r\in\mathbb Q[A,B]$ defined by
\eqref{eq:kappadef} coincides with the constant $\Psi_r(\pi/2)$ of the
phase expansion \eqref{eq:quantisation}.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-57: body_md -->
Both sides are polynomials in $(A,B)$ of degree at most $2r-1\le15$ in
each variable: for \eqref{eq:kappadef} this is
Lemma~\ref{lem:degree}, and $\Psi_r(\pi/2)$ is obtained from the phase
recursion as an explicit polynomial, whose degrees are read off.  The
two polynomials have been evaluated in exact rational arithmetic on the
$16\times16$ product grid $A=i^2/4$, $B=j^2/9$, $1\le i,j\le16$, on
which they agree for every $r\le8$; since a polynomial of degree at
most $15$ in each variable is determined by its values on such a grid,
they coincide.
<!-- end proof-57 -->
<!-- theorem-20: body_md -->
\label{thm:layerexp}
For all parameters $a,b,a',b'$ and generic $c$, as an identity of formal
double series in $x,y$,
\begin{multline}\label{eq:BC}
  \sum_{\mu,\nu\ge0}\frac{(a)_\mu(b)_\mu(a')_\nu(b')_\nu}
       {(c)_{\mu+\nu}\,\mu!\,\nu!}x^\mu y^\nu
  ={}\sum_{r\ge0}\frac{(-1)^r(a)_r(b)_r(a')_r(b')_r}
       {r!\,(c)_{2r}\,(c+r-1)_r}\,(xy)^r\\
  \times\operatorname{{}_2F_1}(a{+}r,b{+}r;c{+}2r;x)\,\operatorname{{}_2F_1}(a'{+}r,b'{+}r;c{+}2r;y).
\end{multline}
<!-- end theorem-20 -->
<!-- proof-58: body_md -->
Comparing coefficients of $x^\mu y^\nu$ and cancelling
$(a)_r(a+r)_{\mu-r}=(a)_\mu$ and its three companions (the parameter
dependence cancels termwise), the claim is equivalent to the pure
identity
\begin{gather}\label{eq:pure}
  \sum_{r=0}^{\min(\mu,\nu)}t_r=\frac1{(c)_{\mu+\nu}\,\mu!\,\nu!},\\
  t_r=\frac{(-1)^r}
      {r!\,(c)_{2r}(c+r-1)_r\,(c+2r)_{\mu-r}(c+2r)_{\nu-r}\,
       (\mu-r)!\,(\nu-r)!}.\notag
\end{gather}
Set $f(\mu,r)=t_r\,(c)_{\mu+\nu}\,\mu!\,\nu!$, extended to real $r$ by
$1/(\mu-r)!=1/\Gamma(\mu-r+1)$ and $1/(\nu-r)!=1/\Gamma(\nu-r+1)$; the
claim is $\Sigma(\mu):=\sum_rf(\mu,r)=1$.  The certificate
\[
  R(r)=-\,\frac{r\,(c+\nu+r-1)}{(c+2r-1)(\mu+1-r)},\qquad h(r)=R(r)f(\mu,r),
\]
satisfies the rational-function identity
$f(\mu+1,r)-f(\mu,r)=h(r+1)-h(r)$ (after division by $f(\mu,r)$ both sides
are rational functions of $r$, and the identity is checked by clearing
denominators).  Both sides are finite
at every integer $r\ge0$: the only delicate points are the simple zeros of
$1/\Gamma$ against the simple pole of $R$ at $r=\mu+1$, where the limits
exist and the identity holds by continuity.  Summing over
$0\le r\le K$, $K=\min(\mu+1,\nu)$, telescopes to
$\Sigma(\mu+1)-\Sigma(\mu)=h(K+1)-h(0)$.  Now $h(0)=0$ since $R(0)=0$; and
$h(K+1)=0$: if $\nu\le\mu$ then $K+1=\nu+1$, where $1/\Gamma(\nu-r+1)$
vanishes and $R$ is regular unless $\mu=\nu$, in which case the double zero
of $1/\bigl(\Gamma(\mu-r+1)\Gamma(\nu-r+1)\bigr)$ beats the simple pole;
if $\nu\ge\mu+1$ then $K+1=\mu+2$, where $1/\Gamma(\mu-r+1)$ vanishes and
$R$ is regular.  Hence $\Sigma(\mu+1)=\Sigma(\mu)$, and $\Sigma(0)=1$.  Symmetry in
$(\mu,\nu)$ completes the induction.
<!-- end proof-58 -->
<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label{cor:layers}
For all $\alpha,\beta$, as formal series in $Z^{-1}$, with
$\gamma_r(A)=(\tfrac12-\alpha)_r(\tfrac12+\alpha)_r
=\prod_{j=0}^{r-1}\bigl((j+\tfrac12)^2-A\bigr)$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:layers}
  F(\alpha,\beta;Z)
  =\sum_{r\ge0}\frac{(-1)^r\,\gamma_r(A)\,\gamma_r(B)}
       {2^{r}\,r!\,(1-Z)_{2r}\,(-Z+r)_r}\;
   \mathcal P_r(A;Z)\;\overline{\mathcal P}_r(B;Z),
\end{equation}
where
$\mathcal P_r(A;Z)=\operatorname{{}_2F_1}(\tfrac12-\alpha+r,\tfrac12+\alpha+r;1-Z+2r;x_0)$
and $\overline{\mathcal P}_r$ is the same series at $y_0=\bar x_0$.  Each
layer is $O(Z^{-3r})$: with $v=1/Z$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rho}
  \frac{(-1)^r\,(x_0y_0)^r}{r!\,(1-Z)_{2r}\,(-Z+r)_r}
  =\frac{v^{3r}}{2^{r}\,r!}\,
   \prod_{j=1}^{2r}\frac1{1-jv}\;\prod_{j=r}^{2r-1}\frac1{1-jv}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- proof-59: body_md -->
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:layerexp} to \eqref{eq:KdF} with $a=\tfrac12-\alpha$,
$b=\tfrac12+\alpha$, $a'=\tfrac12-\beta$, $b'=\tfrac12+\beta$, $c=1-Z$,
$x_0y_0=\tfrac12$, $(c+r-1)_r=(-Z+r)_r$.  Per coefficient of $v^n$ every
sum is finite (the monomial $(\mu,\nu)$ contributes from order $\mu+\nu$
on, the layer $r$ from order $3r$ on), so the rearrangement is
legitimate $v$-adically.  For \eqref{eq:rho} write
$(1-Z+j)=-Z(1-(1+j)v)$ and $(-Z+r+j)=-Z(1-(r+j)v)$.
<!-- end proof-59 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{rem:shape}
At the Legendre point $A=B=0$, $\gamma_r(0)=(\tfrac12)_r^2$ with
$(\tfrac12)_r=(2r)!/(4^rr!)$, so the layer-$r$ prefactor in
\eqref{eq:layers} carries
$\gamma_r(0)^2\,2^{-r}/r!=\bigl((2r)!\bigr)^4/\bigl(2^{\,9r}(r!)^5\bigr)$
against three inverse powers of $Z$ per layer.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
\label{rem:legendre}
$\operatorname{{}_2F_1}(a,1-a;c;x)$ is an associated Legendre function, so
$\mathcal P_0(A;Z)$ is, up to a Gamma-and-power prefactor independent of
$\alpha$, the Legendre function $P^{Z}_{\alpha-1/2}(-i)$ of \emph{order}
$Z$ and degree $\alpha-\frac12$, and its partner is the conjugate function
at $+i$.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- theorem-21: body_md -->
\label{thm:transverse}
Differentiating \eqref{eq:logHornx}--\eqref{eq:logHorny} at $A_-=0$ gives the
exact \emph{linear} forced system
\begin{align}
  Z\mathsf p&=\Theta_x\mathsf h+\mathsf p\mathsf t+\mathsf u\mathsf h
    -x\bigl(\Theta_x\mathsf p+2\mathsf u\mathsf p+\mathsf p-1\bigr),\label{eq:transp}\\
  Z\mathsf q&=\Theta_y\mathsf h+\mathsf q\mathsf t+\mathsf v\mathsf h
    -y\bigl(\Theta_y\mathsf q+2\mathsf v\mathsf q+\mathsf q+1\bigr),\label{eq:transq}
\end{align}
with the compatibility $\Theta_y\mathsf p=\Theta_x\mathsf q$ and forcing
$(x,-y)$.
<!-- end theorem-21 -->
<!-- proof-60: body_md -->
At fixed $A_+$ one has $A=A_++A_-$, $B=A_+-A_-$, hence
$\partial_{A_-}\mu_\alpha=1$ and $\partial_{A_-}\mu_\beta=-1$.  Also
\[
 \partial_{A_-}\mathsf u=\Theta_x\mathcal V_1=\mathsf p,\qquad
 \partial_{A_-}\mathsf v=\Theta_y\mathcal V_1=\mathsf q,\qquad
 \partial_{A_-}\mathsf t=\mathsf h.
\]
Differentiating \eqref{eq:logHornx} term by term therefore gives
\[
 Z\mathsf p
 =\Theta_x\mathsf h+\mathsf p\mathsf t+\mathsf u\mathsf h
  -x\bigl(\Theta_x\mathsf p+2\mathsf u\mathsf p+\mathsf p-1\bigr),
\]
because the derivative of $-\mu_\alpha$ is $-1$.  The $y$ equation is identical
except that $\partial_{A_-}\mu_\beta=-1$, so the derivative of $-\mu_\beta$ is $+1$,
which yields
\[
 Z\mathsf q
 =\Theta_y\mathsf h+\mathsf q\mathsf t+\mathsf v\mathsf h
  -y\bigl(\Theta_y\mathsf q+2\mathsf v\mathsf q+\mathsf q+1\bigr).
\]
Finally, $\Theta_y\mathsf u=\Theta_x\mathsf v$ follows from commutation of
$\Theta_x,\Theta_y$ on $\log F$; differentiating this identity in $A_-$
gives $\Theta_y\mathsf p=\Theta_x\mathsf q$.  Every occurrence of the
unknown transverse quantities is linear, while $\mathsf u,\mathsf v,\mathsf t$ belong to the fixed
diagonal background.
<!-- end proof-60 -->
<!-- corollary-10: body_md -->
\label{cor:transverseunique}
In the class of pairs
\[(\mathsf p,\mathsf q)\in Z^{-1}\,\mathbb C[[x,y]][[Z^{-1}]]^2\]
satisfying the compatibility $\Theta_y\mathsf p=\Theta_x\mathsf q$,
system~\eqref{eq:transp}--\eqref{eq:transq} has at most one solution for the
fixed diagonal background $\mathsf u,\mathsf v,\mathsf t$; hence the solution obtained by differentiating
$\mathcal V_1$ is the unique formal solution with zero constant term in $Z^{-1}$.
<!-- end corollary-10 -->
<!-- proof-61: body_md -->
Existence is already supplied by $\mathsf p=\Theta_x\mathcal V_1$ and
$\mathsf q=\Theta_y\mathcal V_1$.  For uniqueness, let two such solutions be
given and denote their difference by $(\mathsf p^{\circ},\mathsf q^{\circ})$.  The forcing
terms cancel.  Because $F=1+O(Z^{-1})$, one has $\mathsf u,\mathsf v,\mathsf t=O(Z^{-1})$.  Suppose,
for contradiction, that the difference is nonzero and let $n\ge1$ be the
least index for which the coefficient of $Z^{-n}$ in either $\mathsf p^{\circ}$ or
$\mathsf q^{\circ}$ is nonzero.  Multiplication by $Z$ makes the left-hand
side of the corresponding difference equation have a nonzero term of order
$Z^{-(n-1)}$.  Every term on its right-hand side has order at least
$Z^{-n}$: the Euler operators do not change the order in $Z^{-1}$, multiplication
by $x$ or $y$ does not change it, and multiplication by $\mathsf u,\mathsf v,\mathsf t$ raises it by
at least one.  Thus the coefficient of $Z^{-(n-1)}$ on the right is zero, a
contradiction.  Hence $\mathsf p^{\circ}=\mathsf q^{\circ}=0$.
<!-- end proof-61 -->
<!-- corollary-11: body_md -->
\label{cor:Wtransverse}
At the midpoint and at $A_+=0$, write
$\mathcal V_1=\sum_{n\ge1}\mathcal V_{1,n}Z^{-n}$ and
$\widehat{\mathcal V}_1(t)=\sum_{n\ge1}\mathcal V_{1,n}\,t^n/(n-1)!$.
Then, with $W$ as in \eqref{eq:Wdef},
\[
  W(t)=\frac{\sinh2t}{2t^2}\,\operatorname{Im}\widehat{\mathcal V}_1(t).
\]
<!-- end corollary-11 -->
<!-- proof-62: body_md -->
At $A=B=0$,
\[
 \partial_A\log F=\frac12\partial_{A_+}\log F
                    +\frac12\partial_{A_-}\log F.
\]
At the midpoint the first term is real and the second is purely
imaginary.  Passing coefficientwise to the Borel transforms gives
$\operatorname{Im}\Phi(t)=\frac12\operatorname{Im}\widehat{\mathcal V}_1(t)$,
and the formula follows from \eqref{eq:Wdef}.
<!-- end proof-62 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{prop:green}
At $a=0$, with $P_d$, $Q_d$ the Legendre functions of the first and second
kind and $\mathrm h_d=\sum_{j=1}^d1/j$,
\[
  \frac{v_0(x)}{P_d(x)}=\operatorname{artanh}x-\frac{Q_d(x)}{P_d(x)}-\mathrm h_d .
\]
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-63: body_md -->
$P_dQ_d'-Q_dP_d'=(1-x^2)^{-1}$ gives
$(v_0/P_d)'=\frac{P_d^2-1}{(1-x^2)P_d^2}=\frac1{1-x^2}-\bigl(Q_d/P_d\bigr)'$,
so $v_0/P_d=\operatorname{artanh}x-Q_d/P_d+c$.  As $x\to1^-$,
$Q_d(x)=\frac12\log\frac2{1-x}-\mathrm h_d+o(1)$ and
$\operatorname{artanh}x=\frac12\log\frac2{1-x}+o(1)$, while $P_d(1)=1$; hence
$v_0/P_d\to\mathrm h_d+c$, and $v_0(1)=0$ forces $c=-\mathrm h_d$.
<!-- end proof-63 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
\label{rem:mixed}
Proposition~\ref{prop:green} does not give the numbers $g_n$.  With
$\alpha=a+\delta$, $\beta=a-\delta$ one has $A-B=4a\delta$, so
$\partial_\delta(A-B)|_{a=0}=0$: the first $\delta$-variation at $a=0$ does not
move $A-B$ at all.  Since $\kappa_r=(A-B)\,\widetilde\kappa_r(A,B)$ by
\eqref{eq:antisym},
\[
  [A^1B^0]\kappa_r=\widetilde\kappa_r(0,0)
  =\tfrac14\,\partial_a\partial_\delta\,\kappa_r(a+\delta,a-\delta)
   \big|_{a=\delta=0},
\]
a \emph{mixed} derivative.  Moreover the expansion must be taken with
$\mathcal N=d+a+\frac12$ held fixed, not with the degree $d$ held fixed; the two
differ by the variation of the eigenvalue.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- corollary-12: body_md -->
\label{cor:denexp}
$\operatorname{Den}=F(0,0;Z)=\exp\Lambda$, where, by
Theorem~\ref{thm:main} at $\alpha=0$,
\[
  \Lambda(v)=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n\,v^n,\qquad
  \lambda_n=L_n^{\mathrm{diag}}\big|_{\alpha=0}=\frac{4^n}{n(n+1)}
  \Bigl[2\mathcal B_{n+1}\bigl(\tfrac34\bigr)-\mathcal B_{n+1}(1)-\mathcal B_{n+1}\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)
  \Bigr].
\]
<!-- end corollary-12 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{lem:lambda2}
For $k\ge1$,
\[
  \lambda_{2k}=\frac{\mathsf E_{2k}}{4k},\qquad
  \lambda_{2k-1}=-\frac{(2^{2k}-1)\mathcal B_{2k}}{(2k)(2k-1)}.
\]
Hence
\[
  \nu_2(\lambda_{2k})=\nu_2(\lambda_{2k-1})=-2-\nu_2(k);
\]
in particular $\lambda_1=-1/4$, and
$\nu_2(\lambda_n)\ge -n$ for every $n\ge2$.
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-64: body_md -->
By Corollary~\ref{cor:specials}(iii),
\[
  \Upsilon_0(t)=\frac12\left(\operatorname{sech}t
       -\tanh\frac t2-1\right)
  =\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{\lambda_n}{(n-1)!}t^n .
\]
Using
$\operatorname{sech}t=\sum_{k\ge0}\mathsf E_{2k}t^{2k}/(2k)!$ and
$\tanh\frac t2=\sum_{k\ge1}2(2^{2k}-1)\mathcal B_{2k}t^{2k-1}/(2k)!$ gives the
displayed formulas.  Euler numbers are odd, von Staudt--Clausen gives
$\nu_2(\mathcal B_{2k})=-1$, and $2^{2k}-1$ is odd; thus both coefficients
have valuation $-2-\nu_2(k)$.  For $n=2k$ the inequality
$-2-\nu_2(k)\ge-2k$ is $2+\nu_2(k)\le2k$; for
$n=2k-1\ge3$ it is $2+\nu_2(k)\le2k-1$.  Both hold because
$\nu_2(k)\le\log_2k$.
<!-- end proof-64 -->
<!-- theorem-22: body_md -->
\label{thm:lawD}
For every $n\ge0$,
\[
  \nu_2(d_n^{\pm})=-2n-\nu_2(n!) .
\]
Equivalently, $\nu_2(d_{2k}^{\pm})=-\bigl(5k+\nu_2(k!)\bigr)$ and
$\nu_2(d_{2k+1}^{\pm})=-\bigl(5k+2+\nu_2(k!)\bigr)$ for $k\ge0$.
<!-- end theorem-22 -->
<!-- proof-65: body_md -->
Expand the exponential by partitions,
\[
 d_n^{\pm}=\sum_{\substack{m_1,\ldots,m_n\ge0\\
                      \sum_{j=1}^n j m_j=n}}
       \prod_{j=1}^n\frac{(\pm\lambda_j)^{m_j}}{m_j!}.
\]
The partition $m_1=n$, $m_j=0$ for $j\ge2$, contributes
$(\pm\lambda_1)^n/n!$, of valuation $-2n-\nu_2(n!)$.
Consider any other partition and put
$M=\sum_{j\ge2}j m_j>0$, so that $m_1=n-M$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:lambda2}
gives
\begin{align*}
 \nu_2\!\left(\prod_j\frac{\lambda_j^{m_j}}{m_j!}\right)
 &\ge -2m_1-\sum_{j\ge2}jm_j-\sum_j\nu_2(m_j!)
 = -2n+M-\sum_j\nu_2(m_j!).
\end{align*}
The difference with the valuation of the first partition is at least
\[
 M+\nu_2(n!)-\sum_j\nu_2(m_j!)>0,
\]
because $\prod_jm_j!$ divides $(\sum_jm_j)!$, which divides $n!$, while
$M>0$.  Thus exactly one term has minimal valuation, and
$\nu_2(d_n^{\pm})=-2n-\nu_2(n!)$.  Finally
$\nu_2((2k)!)=k+\nu_2(k!)$ and
$\nu_2((2k+1)!)=\nu_2((2k)!)$ give the two other formulas.
<!-- end proof-65 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{prop:lawN}
For every $r,m\ge1$,
\begin{gather*}
  \nu_2\bigl([v^{2r-1}]\operatorname{Im}\operatorname{Num}\bigr)
  =-\bigl(5r-4+\nu_2((r-1)!)\bigr),\\
  \nu_2\bigl([v^{2m}]\operatorname{Im}\operatorname{Num}\bigr)
  =-\bigl(5m-2+\nu_2((m-1)!)\bigr).
\end{gather*}
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-66: body_md -->
By \eqref{eq:tangentformula} and Theorem~\ref{thm:tangentlaw}, in which
$\operatorname{Im}g_{2k}=0$,
\[
 \operatorname{Im}\operatorname{Num}
   =\operatorname{Den}\cdot\sum_{n\ge1}\operatorname{Im}g_n\,v^n
   =\Bigl(\sum_{n\ge0}d_n^+v^n\Bigr)
      \Bigl(\sum_{k\ge1}\operatorname{Im}g_{2k-1}\,v^{2k-1}\Bigr),
\]
so that
\[
 [v^{2r-1}]\operatorname{Im}\operatorname{Num}
   =\sum_{k=1}^r \operatorname{Im}g_{2k-1}\;d_{2(r-k)}^+ .
\]
By Theorems~\ref{thm:tangentlaw} and~\ref{thm:lawD}, the term $k$ has
valuation
$-H_k-5(r-k)-\nu_2((r-k)!)$ with $H_k=k+\nu_2((k-1)!)$.  For $k=1$
this is $-(5r-4+\nu_2((r-1)!))$, and for $2\le k\le r$ it exceeds that
value by
\[
 4(k-1)+\nu_2\binom{r-1}{k-1}>0 .
\]
Hence the term $k=1$ is the only one of minimal valuation, which gives
the first formula.  Similarly,
\[
 [v^{2m}]\operatorname{Im}\operatorname{Num}
   =\sum_{k=1}^m \operatorname{Im}g_{2k-1}\;d_{2(m-k)+1}^+,
\]
where the term $k$ has valuation
$-H_k-5(m-k)-2-\nu_2((m-k)!)$; for $k=1$ this is
$-(5m-2+\nu_2((m-1)!))$, and for $k\ge2$ it exceeds that value by
$4(k-1)+\nu_2\binom{m-1}{k-1}>0$.
<!-- end proof-66 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{prop:congruence}
For $r\ge1$ and $1\le j\le2r-1$ put
\[
  c_{r,j}:=2^{\,5r-4+\nu_2((r-1)!)}\;
  \bigl[v^{j}\bigr]\operatorname{Im}\operatorname{Num}\;\cdot\;
  \bigl[v^{2r-1-j}\bigr]\operatorname{Den}^{-1}.
\]
Then $c_{r,j}\in\mathbb Z_2$,
\begin{gather*}
  \nu_2(c_{r,2k-1})=\nu_2\binom{r-1}{k-1}
  \qquad(1\le k\le r),\\
  \nu_2(c_{r,2k})=1+\nu_2\!\left((r-k)\binom{r-1}{k-1}\right)
  \qquad(1\le k\le r-1),
\end{gather*}
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:lowerbound}
  \sum_{j=1}^{2r-1}c_{r,j}
  =2^{\,5r-4+\nu_2((r-1)!)}\operatorname{Im}g_{2r-1}
  \ \in\ 2^{4(r-1)}\,\mathbb Z_2^\times .
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-67: body_md -->
The two valuation formulas follow from Theorem~\ref{thm:lawD} and
Proposition~\ref{prop:lawN} by addition of exponents: for $j=2k-1$,
\[
 5r-4+\nu_2((r-1)!)-\bigl(5k-4+\nu_2((k-1)!)\bigr)
 -\bigl(5(r-k)+\nu_2((r-k)!)\bigr)=\nu_2\binom{r-1}{k-1},
\]
and for $j=2k$,
\begin{multline*}
 5r-4+\nu_2((r-1)!)-\bigl(5k-2+\nu_2((k-1)!)\bigr)
 -\bigl(5(r-k-1)+2+\nu_2((r-k-1)!)\bigr)\\
 =1+\nu_2\!\left((r-k)\binom{r-1}{k-1}\right).
\end{multline*}
Since $\operatorname{Im}g_{2r-1}
=[v^{2r-1}]\bigl(\operatorname{Im}\operatorname{Num}\cdot
\operatorname{Den}^{-1}\bigr)$, the sum of the $c_{r,j}$ is
$2^{5r-4+\nu_2((r-1)!)}\operatorname{Im}g_{2r-1}$, whose valuation is
$5r-4+\nu_2((r-1)!)-H_r=4(r-1)$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:tangentlaw}.
<!-- end proof-67 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
\label{rem:nonlocal}
The individual terms $c_{r,j}$ have small valuations (at most of the
order of $\log_2r$), whereas their sum is divisible by exactly
$2^{4(r-1)}$.  The valuation of $\operatorname{Im}g_{2r-1}$ therefore
cannot be read off from the individual terms of the convolution
$\operatorname{Im}\operatorname{Num}\cdot\operatorname{Den}^{-1}$.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{lem:hankel}
For all $k\ge0$ and all $\alpha\in\mathbb C$,
\[
 |a_k(\alpha)|\le\cosh(\pi|\alpha|)\,k!\,2^{-k},
\qquad\text{and consequently}\qquad
 |G_n(\alpha)|\le\cosh(\pi|\alpha|)\,(n+1)!\,2^{-n/2}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-68: body_md -->
From the product form
$a_k(\nu)=\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}\bigl(4\nu^2-(2j+1)^2\bigr)/(8^kk!)$,
\[
 |a_k(\alpha)|\le|a_k(0)|
 \prod_{j=0}^{k-1}\Bigl(1+\frac{4|\alpha|^2}{(2j+1)^2}\Bigr)
 \le|a_k(0)|\prod_{j\ge0}\Bigl(1+\frac{4|\alpha|^2}{(2j+1)^2}\Bigr)
 =|a_k(0)|\cosh(\pi|\alpha|),
\]
the last step being the product formula
$\cos(\pi z/2)=\prod_{j\ge0}(1-z^2/(2j+1)^2)$ at $z=2i|\alpha|$.  For
the central value, $|a_k(0)|=\bigl((2k-1)!!\bigr)^2/(8^kk!)$ and
$\bigl((2k-1)!!\bigr)^2\le(2k-1)!!\,(2k)!!=(2k)!$, so
$|a_k(0)|\le(2k)!/(8^kk!)=k!\binom{2k}k8^{-k}
\le k!\,4^k/8^k=k!\,2^{-k}$.
For $G_n$: $|p|=|q|=\sqrt2$ and
$\sum_{l=0}^{n}l!\,(n-l)!\le(n+1)\,n!=(n+1)!$, hence
$|G_n(\alpha)|\le\cosh(\pi|\alpha|)\,2^{n/2}\,2^{-n}\,(n+1)!
=\cosh(\pi|\alpha|)(n+1)!\,2^{-n/2}$.
<!-- end proof-68 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{lem:tailsum}
Let $Z\in\Omega_{\theta_0}$ and $M\ge0$.  Then $(j+1)\le\sqrt2\,|Z-j|$ for
every integer $j\ge0$, and
\[
 \tau_M(Z):=\sum_{n\ge M+1}(n+1)!\,2^{-n/2}
 \prod_{j=M+1}^{n}|Z-j|^{-1}
 \ \le\ (M+1)!\,2^{-M/2}\,\bigl(18|Z|+4\bigr).
\]
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-69: body_md -->
Write $a=\operatorname{Re}Z$, $b=|\operatorname{Im}Z|$, so $|a|\le\theta_0 b$
and $b\ge1/(1-\theta_0)$, i.e.\ $\theta_0 b+1\le b$.  Then
$2|Z-j|^2-(j+1)^2=2(j-a)^2+2b^2-(j+1)^2$; as a function of $j$ this
quadratic has positive leading coefficient and minimum value
$2b^2-2(a+1)^2\ge2b^2-2(\theta_0 b+1)^2\ge0$, which proves
$(j+1)\le\sqrt2|Z-j|$ for all $j\ge0$.  Consequently the terms
$t_n:=(n+1)!\,2^{-n/2}\prod_{j=M+1}^n|Z-j|^{-1}$ satisfy
$t_n/t_{n-1}=(n+1)/(\sqrt2\,|Z-n|)\le1$, so
$t_n\le t_M=(M+1)!\,2^{-M/2}$ for every $n>M$.  Moreover for
$n\ge18|Z|$ one has $|Z-n|\ge n-|Z|\ge n(1-\tfrac1{18})$ and hence
$t_n/t_{n-1}\le\frac{18\,(n+1)}{17\sqrt2\,n}\le\frac45$ once
$n\ge18|Z|\ge18$.  Splitting the sum at $18|Z|$,
\[
 \tau_M\le t_M\bigl(18|Z|\bigr)
 +t_M\sum_{r\ge1}(4/5)^r\le t_M(18|Z|+4).\qedhere
\]
<!-- end proof-69 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
\label{prop:bilateral}
Fix $0<\theta_0<1$.  Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\upshape(i)] the double series \eqref{eq:KdF} converges
absolutely for every $Z\notin\{1,2,3,\dots\}$ and every $\alpha$; its
grouping by $\mu+\nu=n$ is the series $F(\alpha;Z)$ above, which is
therefore analytic in $(\alpha,Z)$ on
$\mathbb C\times(\mathbb C\setminus\{1,2,\dots\})$ and satisfies
\eqref{eq:FH-exact} there;
\item[\upshape(ii)] for every $N$ there are $C_N=C_N(\theta_0)$ and
$y_{\min}=y_{\min}(\theta_0,N)$ such that, uniformly for $Z\in\Omega_{\theta_0}$ and
$|\alpha|\le1$,
\[
 \Bigl|F(\alpha;Z)-\sum_{m=0}^{N}c_m(\alpha)Z^{-m}\Bigr|
 \le C_N\,|Z|^{-N-1},
\]
where $c_m(\alpha)=\sum_{n\le m}G_n(\alpha)\genfrac{\{}{\}}{0pt}{}{m}{n}$ are the plain
coefficients of Lemma~\ref{lem:degree}; the same bound holds for
$\partial_\alpha^kF$ and $\partial_\alpha^kc_m$, $k=1,2$;
\item[\upshape(iii)] consequently, uniformly for $Z\in\Omega_{\theta_0}$
(\emph{both} signs of $\operatorname{Im}Z$),
\[
 \Bigl|\mathcal A(s)-\sum_{n=1}^{N}g_nZ^{-n}\Bigr|\le
 C_N'\,|Z|^{-N-1}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-70: body_md -->
(i) With $|x_0|=|y_0|=2^{-1/2}$, the modulus of the
$(\mu,\nu)$-term of \eqref{eq:KdF} is at most
$C(\alpha)\,\frac{\mu!\,\nu!}{|(1-Z)_{\mu+\nu}|}\,2^{-(\mu+\nu)/2}
\mu^{O(1)}\nu^{O(1)}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:hankel} applied to each
Pochhammer pair, and
$\mu!\,\nu!/(\mu+\nu)!=\binom{\mu+\nu}{\mu}^{-1}\le1$ while
$|(1-Z)_m|\ge c(Z)\,m!\,m^{-\operatorname{Re}Z-1}$ for $m$ large, by
Stirling; the sum over $\mu+\nu=m$ then converges geometrically in
$m$.  Grouping the absolutely convergent double series by $\mu+\nu=n$
gives $G_ne_n$ exactly as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:KdF}.
Identity \eqref{eq:FH-exact} holds for each fixed generic $Z$ by
Theorem~\ref{thm:appellreduce} and \eqref{eq:midpoint2F1}, and both
sides are analytic off the indicated sets, so it holds on the whole
common domain.

(ii) Split $F=\sum_{n\le N}G_ne_n+\mathrm{Rem}_N$.  Each $e_n$, $n\le N$, is
analytic at $Z=\infty$ with
$e_n=\sum_{m=n}^{N}\genfrac{\{}{\}}{0pt}{}{m}{n}Z^{-m}+O_N(|Z|^{-N-1})$ uniformly for
$|Z|\ge2N+2$ (finitely many geometric expansions of
$Z^{-n}\prod_{j\le n}(1-j/Z)^{-1}$), which produces the polynomial part
$\sum_{m\le N}c_mZ^{-m}$ with the stated coefficients plus an error
$O_N(|Z|^{-N-1})$.  For the tail, reserve the first $N+2$ factors:
for $n\ge N+2$,
\[
 \prod_{j=1}^n|Z-j|\ \ge\ |\operatorname{Im}Z|^{\,N+2}
 \prod_{j=N+3}^{n}|Z-j|,
\]
so by Lemmas~\ref{lem:hankel} and~\ref{lem:tailsum} (with $M=N+2$),
\begin{multline*}
 |\mathrm{Rem}_N|\le\sum_{n=N+1}^{N+2}\frac{|G_n|}{|\operatorname{Im}Z|^{\,n}}
 +\frac{\cosh\pi}{|\operatorname{Im}Z|^{N+2}}\,\tau_{N+2}(Z)\\
 \le\frac{C_N''}{|\operatorname{Im}Z|^{N+1}}
 +\frac{C_N'''\,|Z|}{|\operatorname{Im}Z|^{N+2}}
 \le C_N\,|Z|^{-N-1},
\end{multline*}
using $|\operatorname{Im}Z|\ge(1+\theta_0^2)^{-1/2}|Z|$ on $\Omega_{\theta_0}$.
The same argument applies verbatim to
$\partial_\alpha^kF=\sum_n\partial_\alpha^kG_n\,e_n$ after bounding
$|\partial_\alpha^kG_n(\alpha)|\le C(n+1)!\,2^{-n/2}$ for $|\alpha|\le2$
by the Cauchy formula on the circle $|\alpha'-\alpha|=1$ applied to
Lemma~\ref{lem:hankel}; alternatively, apply Cauchy's formula directly
to the remainder $\mathrm{Rem}_N(\alpha;Z)$, which is analytic in $\alpha$.

(iii) $F$ is even in $\alpha$ (each $a_l$ is a function of $\alpha^2$),
so $\partial_\alpha F(0;Z)=0$ and, by \eqref{eq:ND-F},
$\mathcal A=\tfrac12\partial_\alpha^2F(0;Z)/F(0;Z)$.  By (ii),
$F(0;Z)=1+O(|Z|^{-1})$ uniformly on $\Omega_{\theta_0}$, so for
$y_{\min}$ large $|F(0;Z)|\ge\frac12$ and the quotient of the two uniform
expansions is again a uniform expansion, whose coefficients are, by
Corollary~\ref{cor:gausstangent}, exactly $g_n$.
<!-- end proof-70 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
\label{rem:aperture}
The cone $|\operatorname{Re}Z|\le\theta_0|\operatorname{Im}Z|$ with
$\theta_0<1$ cannot be widened by the termwise estimate above: for
directions closer to the real axis the individual terms $G_ne_n$ with
$n\asymp|Z|$ grow exponentially and the series converges only through
cancellation.  The applications of Lemma~\ref{lem:vertical} in this paper
do not require a wider aperture: the matching of
Subsection~\ref{app:sub-imclosed} is performed along a single vertical
line, the decay statements of Subsection~\ref{app:sub-czero} concern
vertical strips, and the coefficients of a Poincar\'e expansion along
one ray are unique.  The mirror symmetry used repeatedly below is the
Schwarz reflection $\mathcal A^{\downarrow}(s)
=\overline{\mathcal A^{\uparrow}(\bar s)}$, valid because all four
blocks $\mathsf S_0,\mathsf K_0,\mathsf S_2,\mathsf K_2$ are real on
the real axis.
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{lem:blocksasy}
Uniformly on every closed subsector of
$|\arg(\pm is)|<\pi/2$, i.e.\ off the real axis, and in particular on
every vertical strip $|\operatorname{Re}s|\le h$,
$|\operatorname{Im}s|\ge1$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\upshape(i)] $\psi'(s)$, $Q_{\rm rat}(s)$ and the convergent
trigamma blocks of \eqref{eq:ReND-closed} are asymptotic to their
(Bernoulli) Stirling series, with remainders
$O_N(|s|^{-N})$ after $N$ terms, and
$|\psi'(s)|+|Q_{\rm rat}(s)|\le C/|\operatorname{Im}s|$;
\item[\upshape(ii)] $\tan\frac{\pi s}2=\pm i+O(e^{-\pi|\operatorname{Im}s|})$
for $\operatorname{Im}s\to\pm\infty$, uniformly in
$\operatorname{Re}s$, and likewise
$\cot\frac{\pi s}2=\mp i+O(e^{-\pi|\operatorname{Im}s|})$,
$\sec^2\frac{\pi s}2$, $\csc^2(\pi s)=O(e^{-\pi|\operatorname{Im}s|})$;
\item[\upshape(iii)] $\widehat{\mathsf r}$ of \eqref{eq:rhatdef} is
asymptotic to its Poincar\'e series \eqref{eq:rhatformal} uniformly on
$|\arg s|\le\pi-\delta$, for every $\delta>0$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-71: body_md -->
(i) and (iii) are Stirling's formula with remainder in sectors
\cite[\S5.11]{DLMF} applied to the explicit Gamma quotients; the decay
bound in (i) follows from $\psi'(z)=O(1/|z|)$ on
$|\operatorname{Im}z|\ge\tfrac12$ together with
$\psi'(z+1)=\psi'(z)-z^{-2}$ to reach the arguments $(1-s)/2$,
$1-s/2$.  (ii) is elementary:
$\tan\frac{\pi s}2\mp i=\mp2i\,e^{\pm i\pi s}/(1+e^{\pm i\pi s})$, and
$|e^{\pm i\pi s}|=e^{-\pi|\operatorname{Im}s|}$ in the indicated
half-planes.
<!-- end proof-71 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{lem:fhatglobal}
Let $\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma$ be \eqref{eq:fgammahat}.  Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\upshape(i)] there is $C$ with
$|\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma(\varsigma)|\le C\,|\varsigma|^{-2}$ uniformly on
$|\operatorname{Im}\varsigma|\ge1$, \emph{including}
$\operatorname{Re}\varsigma\to-\infty$;
\item[\upshape(ii)] for every $M$ there is $C_M$ such that, uniformly on
$\operatorname{Im}\varsigma\ge1$,
\[
 \Bigl|\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma(\varsigma)
 -\sum_{j=2}^{M}\varphi_j\,\varsigma^{-j}\Bigr|
 \le C_M\bigl(|\varsigma|^{-M-1}
 +|\varsigma|^{-2}e^{-\pi\operatorname{Im}\varsigma}\bigr),
\]
where $\sum_j\varphi_j\varsigma^{-j}$ is the formal series
\eqref{eq:fgammahat}; the mirror statement holds for
$\operatorname{Im}\varsigma\le-1$ by
$\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma(\bar\varsigma)
=\overline{\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma(\varsigma)}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-72: body_md -->
Everything reduces to the Gamma quotient in
$\widehat{\mathsf r}(\varsigma)=\varsigma\,
[\Gamma(\varsigma/2)/\Gamma((1+\varsigma)/2)]^2$.  On the right regime
$|\arg\varsigma|\le\tfrac34\pi$, Stirling gives
$\Gamma(\varsigma/2)/\Gamma((1+\varsigma)/2)=(\varsigma/2)^{-1/2}(1+O(1/\varsigma))$
uniformly, whence $|\widehat{\mathsf r}(\varsigma)|\le C$ and the
Poincar\'e expansion \eqref{eq:rhatformal} with uniform remainders
(Lemma~\ref{lem:blocksasy}(iii)).  On the left regime
$\tfrac34\pi\le|\arg\varsigma|\le\pi$, $\operatorname{Im}\varsigma\ge1$,
apply the two reflection formulas used in the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:rhat}:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rhat-left}
 \frac{\Gamma(\varsigma/2)}{\Gamma((1+\varsigma)/2)}
 =\cot\Bigl(\frac{\pi\varsigma}2\Bigr)\,
 \frac{\Gamma\bigl(\frac{1-\varsigma}2\bigr)}
      {\Gamma\bigl(1-\frac\varsigma2\bigr)} ,
\end{equation}
whose right-hand Gamma arguments have real part tending to $+\infty$.
The Beta-integral bound, for $\operatorname{Re}x>0$,
\[
 \Bigl|\frac{\Gamma(x)}{\Gamma(x+\frac12)}\Bigr|
 =\frac{|\mathrm B(x,\tfrac12)|}{\Gamma(\tfrac12)}
 \le\frac{\mathrm B(\operatorname{Re}x,\tfrac12)}{\sqrt\pi}
 \le C\,(\operatorname{Re}x)^{-1/2}
\]
with $x=\frac{1-\varsigma}2$, together with
$\cot(\pi\varsigma/2)=-i+O(e^{-\pi\operatorname{Im}\varsigma})$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:blocksasy}(ii)), gives
$|\widehat{\mathsf r}(\varsigma)|\le C$ on the left regime as well; (i)
follows since
$\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma=-\tfrac{(2\varsigma-1)}{4\varsigma^2(\varsigma-1)}
\widehat{\mathsf r}$.
For (ii): on the left regime, \eqref{eq:rhat-left} squared gives
\[
 \widehat{\mathsf r}(\varsigma)
 =-\varsigma\Bigl[\frac{\Gamma\bigl(\frac{1-\varsigma}2\bigr)}
      {\Gamma\bigl(1-\frac\varsigma2\bigr)}\Bigr]^2
 \bigl(1+O(e^{-\pi\operatorname{Im}\varsigma})\bigr),
\]
and the squared quotient has a uniform Stirling expansion in
$\varsigma^{-1}$ (right half-plane arguments).  The resulting Poincar\'e
series coincides with \eqref{eq:rhatformal}: both are asymptotic
expansions of the same function $\widehat{\mathsf r}$ on the open
overlap sector $\tfrac34\pi<|\arg\varsigma|<\pi-\delta$ (where the cot
correction is exponentially small in $|\varsigma|$), and the coefficients
of a Poincar\'e expansion on a sector are unique.  (Arithmetically the
same coincidence is the parity identity of Lemma~\ref{lem:parityF}.)
Combining the two regimes, with the exponentially small cot correction
retained additively, gives (ii).
<!-- end proof-72 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label{lem:fhatpoles}
$\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma$ is meromorphic on $\mathbb C$ with:
double zeros at the negative odd integers; a pole of order $3$ at
$\varsigma=0$, a simple pole at $\varsigma=1$, double poles at the negative
even integers, and no other poles.  The principal-part coefficients at
$\varsigma=-2m$ are $O(m^{-2})$.  Consequently
$T(s)=\sum_{k\ge0}\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma(s-1-2k)$ converges
normally on compact sets avoiding $\mathbb Z$ and defines a meromorphic
function on $\mathbb C$ with poles contained in $\mathbb Z$;
$T$ has (at least) double zeros at the negative even integers, at most
double poles at the negative odd integers, and satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:T-global}
 |T(s)|\le\frac{C}{|\operatorname{Im}s|},\qquad
 |\operatorname{Im}s|\ge1,
\end{equation}
uniformly in $\operatorname{Re}s$.  Finally
$T(s+2)-T(s)=\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma(s+1)$.
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- proof-73: body_md -->
$\Gamma((1+\varsigma)/2)^{-2}$ has double zeros at
$\varsigma=-1,-3,\dots$; $\Gamma(\varsigma/2)^{2}$ has double poles at
$\varsigma=0,-2,-4,\dots$; combining with the elementary factor
$-(2\varsigma-1)/\bigl(4\varsigma^2(\varsigma-1)\bigr)$ of
\eqref{eq:fgammahat} gives the stated orders (at $\varsigma=0$:
$\widehat{\mathsf r}\sim4/(\pi\varsigma)$, so
$\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma\sim-1/(\pi\varsigma^3)$; at $\varsigma=1$:
$\widehat{\mathsf r}(1)=\pi$).  At $\varsigma=-2m$ the double-pole
coefficient of $\widehat{\mathsf r}$ is
$-8m\,\Gamma(m+\tfrac12)^2/\bigl(\pi^2(m!)^2\bigr)=O(1)$ by the
reflection formula, and the elementary factor contributes an extra
$O(m^{-2})$.  The term $\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma(s-1-2k)$ of $T$ has
poles only at integers: at $s=1+2k$, at $s=2+2k$, and at the odd
integers $s=1+2k-2m$, $m\ge1$, where it has a double pole with
principal-part coefficients $O(m^{-2})$.  At a fixed odd integer these
coefficients are therefore summable in $k$, and away from small discs
around the integers the terms are dominated by
Lemma~\ref{lem:fhatglobal}(i); this gives normal convergence and
meromorphy, and shows that $T$ has at most double poles at the negative
odd integers.  The double zeros of $T$ at $s=-2m$ hold
because every term is then evaluated at a negative odd integer, where
$\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma$ has a double zero as a function of $s$.
For \eqref{eq:T-global}: with $\operatorname{Im}s=Y$, $|Y|\ge1$, all
lattice points $\varsigma_k=s-1-2k$ have $|\operatorname{Im}\varsigma_k|=|Y|$,
so by Lemma~\ref{lem:fhatglobal}(i),
$|T|\le C\sum_{k\ge0}\bigl(Y^2+(\operatorname{Re}s-1-2k)^2\bigr)^{-1}
\le C'/|Y|$ by comparison with
$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(Y^2+u^2)^{-1}du=\pi/|Y|$.  The difference
equation is immediate from the definition.
<!-- end proof-73 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
\label{prop:latticetail}
Let $\omega_j$ be the coefficients of the formal series
$\widehat Q_\Gamma=(2\sinh\partial_s)^{-1}\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma\in
s^{-1}\mathbb Q[[s^{-1}]]$ of \eqref{eq:Qgammahat}.  For every
$\delta>0$ and every $N$ there are $C_{\delta,N}$ and $s_{\min}$ such that,
uniformly on the sector
$\operatorname{Im}s\ge\delta|s|$, $|s|\ge s_{\min}$,
\[
 \Bigl|T(s)-\sum_{j=1}^{N}\omega_j\,s^{-j}\Bigr|
 \ \le\ C_{\delta,N}\,|s|^{-N-1}
 \ +\ C_\delta\,\frac{e^{-\pi\operatorname{Im}s}}{\operatorname{Im}s}.
\]
The mirror statement holds on $\operatorname{Im}s\le-\delta|s|$ with
the same (rational) coefficients, by Schwarz reflection.
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- proof-74: body_md -->
Fix $M\ge N+2$.  Insert Lemma~\ref{lem:fhatglobal}(ii) termwise:
\[
 T(s)=\sum_{j=2}^{M}\varphi_j\,\Sigma_j(s)+\mathrm{Err}_1+\mathrm{Err}_2,
 \qquad
 \Sigma_j(s):=\sum_{k\ge0}(s-1-2k)^{-j},
\]
with
$|\mathrm{Err}_1|\le C_M\sum_{k\ge0}|s-1-2k|^{-M-1}$ and
$|\mathrm{Err}_2|\le C\,e^{-\pi\operatorname{Im}s}
\sum_{k\ge0}|s-1-2k|^{-2}$.  For the error sums split at
$k\le|s|$ and $k>|s|$: the near terms number at most $|s|+1$ and each
is at most $(\operatorname{Im}s)^{-M-1}\le(\delta|s|)^{-M-1}$, giving
$\le2\delta^{-M-1}|s|^{-M}$; the far terms are dominated by
$\sum_{k>|s|}(2k-1-|s|)^{-M-1}\le C|s|^{-M}$.  Hence
$|\mathrm{Err}_1|\le C_{\delta,M}'|s|^{-M}$, and similarly
$|\mathrm{Err}_2|\le C_\delta\,e^{-\pi\operatorname{Im}s}/\operatorname{Im}s$ as
in \eqref{eq:T-global}.  Next, with $a=(1-s)/2$ (which satisfies
$|\arg a|\le\pi-\delta'$, $\delta'=\delta'(\delta)>0$, on the sector),
\[
 \Sigma_j(s)=(-2)^{-j}\,\zeta(j,a),
\]
and the Hurwitz zeta function has the classical uniform large-$a$
expansion \cite[\S25.11(xii)]{DLMF}
\[
 \zeta(j,a)=\frac{a^{1-j}}{j-1}+\frac{a^{-j}}2
 +\sum_{r=1}^{R}\binom{j+2r-2}{2r-1}\frac{\mathcal B_{2r}}{2r}\,a^{-j-2r+1}
 +O_{j,R}\bigl(|a|^{-j-2R-1}\bigr)
\]
uniformly on $|\arg a|\le\pi-\delta'$.  Substituting these finitely
many expansions (each truncated at total order $N+1$ in $s^{-1}$) and
re-expanding $a=(1-s)/2$ in powers of $s^{-1}$ produces a fixed formal
series $\widehat T=\sum_j\hat\omega_js^{-j}$, with no constant term (the
leading contribution of $\Sigma_j$ is of order $s^{1-j}$ and
$\varphi_j$ starts at $j=2$), such that
$T(s)=\sum_{j\le N}\hat\omega_js^{-j}+O_{\delta,N}(|s|^{-N-1})
+O_\delta(e^{-\pi\operatorname{Im}s}/\operatorname{Im}s)$ on the
sector.  It remains to identify $\widehat T=\widehat Q_\Gamma$.  The
exact difference equation $T(s+2)-T(s)=\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma(s+1)$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:fhatpoles}), the uniform expansion just proved (applied
at $s$ and $s+2$, both in the sector), and
Lemma~\ref{lem:fhatglobal}(ii) at $\varsigma=s+1$ force the coefficientwise
identity $\widehat T(s+2)-\widehat T(s)
=\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma$-series$(s+1)$; equivalently, in the
shifted variable $u=s+1$, $\widehat T(u+1)-\widehat T(u-1)$ equals the
series \eqref{eq:fgammahat} at $u$.  By
Proposition~\ref{prop:formal-sinh} the unique solution of this
equation in $s^{-1}\mathbb Q[[s^{-1}]]$ is $\widehat Q_\Gamma$, so
$\widehat T=\widehat Q_\Gamma$ and $\hat\omega_j=\omega_j$.
<!-- end proof-74 -->
<!-- lemma-27: body_md -->
\label{lem:tworelation}
As an identity of meromorphic functions on $\mathbb C$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tworelation}
 \Bigl(\tan\frac{\pi s}2-i\Bigr)\mathcal A^{\uparrow}(s)
 +\Bigl(\tan\frac{\pi s}2+i\Bigr)\mathcal A^{\downarrow}(s)
 =\tan\frac{\pi s}2\,\Bigl(Q(s)-\frac{\psi'(s)}2\Bigr),
\end{equation}
with $Q=\mathsf K_2/\mathsf K_0$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm:quad}.
<!-- end lemma-27 -->
<!-- proof-75: body_md -->
Write $\mathfrak t=\tan\frac{\pi s}2=\pi\mathsf K_0/\mathsf S_0$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:quadeval}).  From $1+i\mathfrak t=i(\mathfrak t-i)$ and
$1-i\mathfrak t=-i(\mathfrak t+i)$,
\[
 \frac{\mathfrak t-i}{1+i\mathfrak t}=-i,\qquad
 \frac{\mathfrak t+i}{1-i\mathfrak t}=i .
\]
Hence
\[
 (\mathfrak t-i)\,\frac{\mathsf S_2+i\pi\mathsf K_2}{\mathsf S_0(1+i\mathfrak t)}
 +(\mathfrak t+i)\,\frac{\mathsf S_2-i\pi\mathsf K_2}{\mathsf S_0(1-i\mathfrak t)}
 =\frac{-i(\mathsf S_2+i\pi\mathsf K_2)+i(\mathsf S_2-i\pi\mathsf K_2)}
 {\mathsf S_0}
 =\frac{2\pi\mathsf K_2}{\mathsf S_0}
 =2\mathfrak t\,Q ,
\]
and adding the $-\psi'/4$ parts, whose coefficients sum to $2\mathfrak t$,
gives \eqref{eq:tworelation}.
<!-- end proof-75 -->
<!-- corollary-13: body_md -->
\label{cor:Qvert}
For every $h>0$ there are $C(h)$ and $y'_{\min}(h)$ with
\[
 |Q(s)|\le\frac{C(h)}{|\operatorname{Im}s|},
 \qquad |\operatorname{Re}s|\le h,\
 |\operatorname{Im}s|\ge y'_{\min}(h),
\]
uniformly on the strip; in particular $Q\to0$ at both vertical ends of
every strip, uniformly in $\operatorname{Re}s$ on compact sets.
<!-- end corollary-13 -->
<!-- proof-76: body_md -->
Solve \eqref{eq:tworelation} for $Q$:
\[
 Q=\frac{\psi'(s)}2+\frac{(\mathfrak t-i)\mathcal A^{\uparrow}
 +(\mathfrak t+i)\mathcal A^{\downarrow}}{\mathfrak t}.
\]
The vertical strip $|\operatorname{Re}s|\le h$,
$|\operatorname{Im}s|\ge y'_{\min}$ maps under $Z=1-2s$ into
$\Omega_{1/2}$ once $y'_{\min}\ge2(2h+1)$ and $y'_{\min}$ is at least
the threshold of Proposition~\ref{prop:bilateral}, so
Proposition~\ref{prop:bilateral}(iii) with $N=1$ gives
$|\mathcal A^{\uparrow}(s)|\le C/|Z|\le C'/|\operatorname{Im}s|$ there;
the same bound holds for $\mathcal A^{\downarrow}(s)
=\overline{\mathcal A^{\uparrow}(\bar s)}$ since $\bar s$ lies in the
mirror strip.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:blocksasy},
$|\psi'(s)|\le C/|\operatorname{Im}s|$,
$|\mathfrak t\mp i|\le3e^{-\pi|\operatorname{Im}s|}$ (for $\operatorname{Im}s\to\pm\infty$ respectively) and
$|\mathfrak t|\ge\tfrac12$ for $|\operatorname{Im}s|\ge1$.  The claim follows.
<!-- end proof-76 -->
<!-- lemma-28: body_md -->
\label{lem:cylclass}
Let $f$ be meromorphic on $\mathbb C$, $2$-periodic, with all poles
contained in $\mathbb Z$, of order at most $k_1$ at the odd integers and
at most $k_0$ at the even integers, and suppose that
$f(s)\to0$ as $\operatorname{Im}s\to+\infty$ and as
$\operatorname{Im}s\to-\infty$, uniformly for
$\operatorname{Re}s\in[0,2]$.  Then
\[
 f(s)=\frac{w\,n_1(w)}{(w+1)^{k_1}\,(w-1)^{k_0}},\qquad w=e^{i\pi s},
\]
with $n_1$ a polynomial of degree at most $k_1+k_0-2$ (and $f\equiv0$
when $k_1+k_0\le1$).  In particular, if $k_1\le1$ and $k_0=0$ then
$f\equiv0$; if $k_1=2$ and $k_0=0$ then
$f\in\mathbb C\cdot\sec^2\frac{\pi s}2$.
<!-- end lemma-28 -->
<!-- proof-77: body_md -->
The map $s\mapsto w=e^{i\pi s}$ identifies the cylinder
$\mathbb C/2\mathbb Z$ with $\mathbb C^*$; a $2$-periodic meromorphic
function $f$ is therefore of the form $f(s)=R(e^{i\pi s})$ with $R$
meromorphic on $\mathbb C^*$.  The poles of $f$ correspond to $w=-1$
(odd integers) and $w=+1$ (even integers), with the stated orders,
since $w\mp1$ vanishes to first order in $s$ at the corresponding
integers.  The end $\operatorname{Im}s\to+\infty$ is $w\to0$ and the
end $\operatorname{Im}s\to-\infty$ is $w\to\infty$; the hypothesis says
that $R(w)\to0$ as $w\to0$ and as $w\to\infty$ (uniform decay on one
period suffices, every $w$ near $0$ or $\infty$ having a preimage with
$\operatorname{Re}s\in[0,2]$).  Hence $R$ is bounded near $0$ and
$\infty$, these singularities are removable with value $0$, and $R$ is
meromorphic on the Riemann sphere, that is, rational, with poles only
at $-1$ and $+1$, of orders at most $k_1$ and $k_0$.  Thus
$R=n_0(w)/((w+1)^{k_1}(w-1)^{k_0})$ with a polynomial $n_0$ of degree at
most $k_1+k_0-1$ (zero at $\infty$) and $n_0(0)=0$ (zero at $0$): hence
$n_0=w\,n_1$ with $\deg n_1\le k_1+k_0-2$.  For $k_1=2$, $k_0=0$ this is
$R=c\,w/(w+1)^2$, and $4w/(w+1)^2=\sec^2\frac{\pi s}2$.
<!-- end proof-77 -->
<!-- theorem-23: body_md -->
\label{thm:czero}
Define
\[
 \mathcal D(s):=Q(s)-Q_{\rm rat}(s)+\cot\frac{\pi s}2\;T(s).
\]
Then $\mathcal D\equiv0$.  Equivalently, in the decomposition
\eqref{eq:Qdecomp} one has $c_*(s_0)=0$ for every admissible step-two
lattice, real or complex, and \eqref{eq:Edef} holds with $c_*(s_0)=0$.
<!-- end theorem-23 -->
<!-- proof-78: body_md -->
\emph{$\mathcal D$ is meromorphic with poles in $\mathbb Z$.}
$\mathsf K_0=\Gamma(1+\tfrac s2)/(\Gamma(1+s)\Gamma(1-\tfrac s2))$ is
entire, with zeros exactly at the negative odd integers and the positive
even integers.  $\mathsf K_2$ is analytic on
$\operatorname{Re}s<\tfrac12$: the defining series converges locally
uniformly there; at a nonpositive integer $s=-m$ the only singular
inner terms are those with $j=m$, present exactly for $n\ge m+1$, and
there the double zero of $((s)_n/n!)^2$ at $s=-m$ cancels the double
pole of $(s+m)^{-2}$, while the finitely many terms with $n\le m$
contain no factor $(s+m)^{-2}$.  It extends meromorphically to
$\mathbb C$ by the recurrence \eqref{eq:K2rec}, whose coefficients
vanish only at integers.  Hence $Q=\mathsf K_2/\mathsf K_0$ is
meromorphic with poles in $\mathbb Z$; so are $Q_{\rm rat}$,
$\cot\frac{\pi s}2$ and $T$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:fhatpoles}).

\emph{$\mathcal D$ is $2$-periodic.}  By \eqref{eq:Qdiff} at $s+1$,
$Q(s+2)-Q(s)=\mathsf f(s+1)$; by the trigamma recurrence,
$Q_{\rm rat}(s+2)-Q_{\rm rat}(s)=\mathsf f_{\rm rat}(s+1)$; by
Lemma~\ref{lem:fhatpoles},
$T(s+2)-T(s)=\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma(s+1)$; and
$\tan\frac{\pi(s+1)}2=-\cot\frac{\pi s}2$, so
$\mathsf f_\Gamma(s+1)
=-\cot\frac{\pi s}2\,\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma(s+1)$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:rhat}).  Hence
\[
 \mathcal D(s+2)-\mathcal D(s)=\mathsf f(s+1)-\mathsf f_{\rm rat}(s+1)
 +\cot\frac{\pi s}2\,\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma(s+1)
 =\mathsf f_\Gamma(s+1)
 +\cot\frac{\pi s}2\,\widehat{\mathsf f}_\Gamma(s+1)=0 .
\]

\emph{Pole orders.}  Because $\mathcal D$ is $2$-periodic, the pole
order on each residue class may be read off at any one representative.
At $s=-2m$, $m\ge1$: $\mathsf K_0(-2m)=(-1)^m\binom{2m}m\ne0$ and
$\mathsf K_2$ is analytic there, so $Q$ is analytic;
$Q_{\rm rat}$ is analytic (its trigamma arguments are
$\tfrac12+m$ and $1+m$); and the simple pole of $\cot\frac{\pi s}2$ is
cancelled by the double zero of $T$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:fhatpoles}).  Hence
$\mathcal D$ is analytic on the even class.  At $s=-(2m+1)$:
$\mathsf K_0$ has a simple zero and $\mathsf K_2$ is analytic, so $Q$
has at most a simple pole; $Q_{\rm rat}$ is analytic; and
$\cot\frac{\pi s}2$ has a simple zero, while $T$ has at most a double
pole.  Hence $\mathcal D$ has at most a simple pole on the odd class.

\emph{Decay at the ends.}  On the strip
$\operatorname{Re}s\in[0,2]$, $|\operatorname{Im}s|\ge y'_{\min}$, there
is a constant $c$ such that
$|Q|\le c/|\operatorname{Im}s|$ by Corollary~\ref{cor:Qvert},
$|Q_{\rm rat}|\le c/|\operatorname{Im}s|$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:blocksasy}(i), and $|T|\le c/|\operatorname{Im}s|$ by
\eqref{eq:T-global}, while $\cot\frac{\pi s}2$ is bounded.  Hence
$\mathcal D(s)\to0$ uniformly on the strip as
$\operatorname{Im}s\to\pm\infty$.

By Lemma~\ref{lem:cylclass} with $k_1=1$, $k_0=0$,
$\mathcal D\equiv0$.  On any step-two lattice $\{s_0-2k\}$ avoiding the
poles, comparison with \eqref{eq:Qdecomp} gives
$c_*(s_0)=\mathcal D(s_0)=0$.
<!-- end proof-78 -->
<!-- corollary-14: body_md -->
\label{cor:Edef-czero}
In Proposition~\ref{prop:osc-remainder} the remainder \eqref{eq:Edef}
is
$\mathcal E(s)=\tfrac12Q_{\rm rat}(s)-\operatorname{Re}\mathcal A-\tfrac14\psi'(s)$, with no lattice term; and the two-component
relation takes the closed form
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tworelation-X}
 \Bigl(\tan\frac{\pi s}2-i\Bigr)\mathcal A^{\uparrow}
 +\Bigl(\tan\frac{\pi s}2+i\Bigr)\mathcal A^{\downarrow}
 =-\,T(s)+\tan\frac{\pi s}2\,
 \Bigl(Q_{\rm rat}(s)-\frac{\psi'(s)}2\Bigr)=:X(s).
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-14 -->
<!-- proof-79: body_md -->
Insert $Q=Q_{\rm rat}-\cot\frac{\pi s}2\,T$
(Theorem~\ref{thm:czero}) into \eqref{eq:tworelation} and use
$\tan\cdot\cot=1$.
<!-- end proof-79 -->
<!-- lemma-29: body_md -->
\label{lem:stirparity}
As an identity in $\mathbb Q[[s^{-1}]]$, with the left side re-expanded
in powers of $s^{-1}$,
\[
 S_\psi(1-s)=-S_\psi(s).
\]
<!-- end lemma-29 -->
<!-- proof-80: body_md -->
Work in the Borel (Watson) picture, in which
$\sum_nc_ns^{-n-1}$ corresponds to the kernel $\sum_nc_nt^n/n!$ and a
shift $s\mapsto s-a$ corresponds, exactly and coefficientwise, to
multiplication of the kernel by $e^{at}$.  The kernel of $S_\psi$ is
$\varphi_\psi(t)=t/(1-e^{-t})$.  First,
$\varphi_\psi(t)(1-e^{t})=-te^{t}$ is the kernel of $-\sum_{n\ge1}ns^{-n-1}
=-(s-1)^{-2}$, i.e.
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Spsi-rec}
 S_\psi(s)-S_\psi(s-1)=-(s-1)^{-2}
\end{equation}
coefficientwise.  Second, directly from the parity of the
coefficients, $S_\psi(-x)+S_\psi(x)=x^{-2}$.  Applying this at
$x=s-1$ and then \eqref{eq:Spsi-rec},
\[
 S_\psi(1-s)=-S_\psi(s-1)+(s-1)^{-2}
 =-\bigl[S_\psi(s)+(s-1)^{-2}\bigr]+(s-1)^{-2}=-S_\psi(s).
\]
<!-- end proof-80 -->
<!-- proof-81: body_md -->
All expansions below are along the vertical line
$s=-\tfrac12+iY$, $Y\to-\infty$; recall that the coefficients of a
Poincar\'e expansion along a single ray are unique, so establishing
\eqref{eq:formal-tangent} there establishes it as an identity of formal
series.  The line lies, for $Z=1-2s$, in $\Omega_{1/2}$, and in the
sector $\operatorname{Im}s\le-\tfrac12|s|$ for $|Y|\ge1$.

By Proposition~\ref{prop:bilateral}(iii),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:match-1}
 \mathcal A^{\uparrow}(s)=\sum_{n=1}^Ng_nZ^{-n}+O(|Z|^{-N-1}),
\end{equation}
and $\mathcal A^{\downarrow}(s)
=\overline{\mathcal A^{\uparrow}(\bar s)}=O(|Z|^{-1})$ since $\bar s$
lies in the mirror line.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:blocksasy}(ii),
$\tan\frac{\pi s}2+i=O(e^{-\pi|Y|})$ and
$\tan\frac{\pi s}2-i=-2i+O(e^{-\pi|Y|})$.  The right side of
\eqref{eq:tworelation-X} is $O(1/|Y|)$ by \eqref{eq:T-global} and
Lemma~\ref{lem:blocksasy}(i).  Hence, solving
\eqref{eq:tworelation-X} for $\mathcal A^{\uparrow}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:match-2}
 \mathcal A^{\uparrow}(s)=\frac{X(s)}{-2i}+O\bigl(e^{-\pi|Y|}\bigr)
 =\frac i2X(s)+O\bigl(e^{-\pi|Y|}\bigr).
\end{equation}
Now expand $X$.  By the mirror statement of
Proposition~\ref{prop:latticetail} (with $\delta=\tfrac12$),
$T(s)=\sum_{j\le N}\omega_js^{-j}+O(|s|^{-N-1})+O(e^{-\pi|Y|})$, with
$\sum \omega_js^{-j}=\widehat Q_\Gamma$; by Lemma~\ref{lem:blocksasy}(i)
and Corollary~\ref{cor:rational-quadrature}, $Q_{\rm rat}$ and
$\psi'$ are asymptotic to their Stirling series, the former to the
unique formal solution of its central-difference equation; and
$\tan\frac{\pi s}2=-i+O(e^{-\pi|Y|})$.  Therefore
\[
 X(s)=-\widehat Q_\Gamma(s)
 -i\Bigl(Q_{\rm rat}^{\rm ser}(s)-\tfrac12S_\psi(s)\Bigr)
 +O(|s|^{-N-1})+O(e^{-\pi|Y|})
\]
in the obvious truncated sense, where $Q_{\rm rat}^{\rm ser}$ denotes
the (rational-coefficient) Stirling series of \eqref{eq:Qrat}.
Combining with \eqref{eq:match-1}--\eqref{eq:match-2} and equating
coefficients along the line,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:match-3}
 \sum_{n\ge1}g_nZ^{-n}
 =\frac12\,Q_{\rm rat}^{\rm ser}(s)-\frac14\,S_\psi(s)
 -\frac i2\,\widehat Q_\Gamma(s),
\end{equation}
all three series on the right being re-expanded in $Z^{-1}$ through the
exact substitution $s=(1-Z)/2$.  The three series have rational
coefficients, so the splitting of \eqref{eq:match-3} into real and
imaginary parts is coefficientwise:
$\operatorname{Im}g_n=-\tfrac12\widehat q_n$, which is
\eqref{eq:Imgclosed}, and
$\sum\operatorname{Re}g_nZ^{-n}
=\tfrac12Q_{\rm rat}^{\rm ser}-\tfrac14S_\psi(s)$.  For the real part,
$\tfrac12Q_{\rm rat}^{\rm ser}
=\tfrac1{16}\psi'\bigl(\tfrac{Z+1}4\bigr)
-\tfrac1{16}\psi'\bigl(\tfrac{Z+3}4\bigr)$ as Bernoulli series (the
arguments $(1-s)/2$ and $1-s/2$ equal $(Z+1)/4$ and $(Z+3)/4$), while
Lemma~\ref{lem:stirparity} gives
$-\tfrac14S_\psi(s)=\tfrac14S_\psi(1-s)
=\tfrac14\psi'\bigl(\tfrac{Z+1}2\bigr)$ as Bernoulli series
($1-s=(Z+1)/2$); so the real part of \eqref{eq:match-3} is exactly
\eqref{eq:realkernel}, in agreement with
Theorem~\ref{thm:realkernel}.  This proves
\eqref{eq:formal-tangent}.
<!-- end proof-81 -->
